`pin` for a badge that has one), before the attempt is reserved, so a blocked attempt costs the
badge's own count nothing. Badge-only sign-in, the PIN challenge and unknown-badge handling never
read or charge it, and it is separate from the route's unknown-badge throttle (8 per 15 minutes; see
[Rate Limiting](#rate-limiting)), which no PIN outcome charges. Like the other login throttles it
fails open when its counter store is unavailable. The station-gated crew mint charges no IP at all.

**What a shop behind one NAT address sees.** Desks and solo kiosks in one building usually share an
egress address, and so share this budget. Correct sign-ins never spend it, so ordinary use costs
nothing. If 60 wrong PINs (and attempts against locked PINs) pile up from that address within 15
minutes, by a bad morning of fumbled PINs or by someone sweeping badges, **PIN sign-in from that
address pauses for up to 15 minutes**: every badge whose user has a PIN gets the **429** at the desk
and the solo kiosk. Badges without a PIN (where the policy allows it), password sign-in and the
crew stations are unaffected.

- **`detail` is an object** for the coded answers (`floor_pin_required`, `floor_pin_not_set`,
  `floor_pin_reset_required`, and on any session `floor_pin_reauth_required`, below); read
  `detail.code`, never the HTTP status alone (a 401 without a code is a refusal: an unknown badge,
  or a wrong or locked PIN). The one client implementation is
  `frontend/src/services/badgeSignOn.ts` (`signOnWithBadge`). It always shows the one text "Invalid
  badge or PIN" on a refused PIN, whatever the server sent, and shows a 429 on the pad, which then
  takes no more PINs and offers only Back. The SPA's axios interceptor treats an `employee-login`
  401 as an answer, never as a reason to refresh or sign out.
- **The PIN is a credential.** It is stored only as a bcrypt hash (`users.floor_pin_hash`), never
  serialized, logged, audited or echoed. The request field coerces any JSON value to a string, so a
  malformed `pin` is never refused by the schema; it is read as a wrong PIN and counts as one. A 422
  never echoes a PIN either: the validation handler replaces the value of any `pin` / `new_pin` /
  `floor_pin` key with `"[redacted]"`, at any depth of an error's `input` (see
  [Validation Error (422)](#validation-error-422)). The sign-on step never binds the stored hash to a
  local variable, Sentry events are scrubbed of PINs, hashes, raw request bodies and SQL parameters
  (see [ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLES.md → Monitoring](ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLES.md#monitoring--error-tracking)),
  and no audit row carries `floor_pin_hash` (`AuditService` drops it from every model snapshot).
- **Its own lock, and race-safe.** `floor_pin_failed_attempts` / `floor_pin_locked_until` are
  separate from the password lockout (`failed_login_attempts` / `locked_until`) in both directions:
  a PIN lock never locks the person's password login, and `POST /users/{id}/unlock` does not clear
  a PIN lock. It is one count per person across both routes. Each attempt is **reserved before the
  PIN is checked**: one conditional `UPDATE` counts it, and sets the tier's lock when the count
  reaches one, unless a lock is in force; that count is committed before bcrypt runs, so racing
  attempts on one badge each spend their own guess and a lost audit row or a crash never gives one
  back. A right PIN then settles by compare-and-set (`WHERE` the count is still the one it
  reserved): it clears the count and any lock its own attempt set, keeps a racing attempt's count
  when another reserved meanwhile, and is refused as locked only when one of those locked the PIN.
  A lock in force is never extended or shortened by later attempts.
- **Audit rows.** `employee-login` writes `EMPLOYEE_LOGIN_FAILED` / `EMPLOYEE_LOGIN_SUCCESS` (and
  `EMPLOYEE_LOGIN_BLOCKED` for the per-IP PIN block); the mint writes `KIOSK_BADGE_TOKEN_FAILED` /
  `KIOSK_BADGE_TOKEN_ISSUED`, station-keyed as before, its PIN failures adding
  `extra_data.badge_user_id`. Both success rows carry `extra_data.auth_methods`.
- **Rollout.** After the upgrade no user has a PIN and every company is off, so both routes answer
  exactly as before. PINs are set by an Admin, or by a Manager for Operator / Supervisor / Shipping
  / Viewer accounts (`PUT /users/{user_id}/floor-pin`, see [Users](#users-admin)); the policy by an
  Admin (`PUT /companies/me/floor-pin-policy`, see
  [Company](#company-self-service)). There is no self-service PIN change, and the PIN is asked at
  sign-on only, not again at an inspection sign-off.

**The `amr` and `pst` claims.** Both routes mint an RFC 8176 `amr` (authentication methods
reference) claim: `["badge", "pin"]` when a PIN was verified, `["badge"]` otherwise (on
`employee-login`, in the access and the refresh token). A `["badge", "pin"]` session also carries
**`pst`**, the verified PIN's `floor_pin_set_at` as integer epoch-microseconds, which binds the
session to that PIN (below). Both are written **only** by badge sign-on: `POST /auth/login`
(password, including an employee ID plus password) and registration mint exactly
the claims they always did. `get_current_user` copies `amr` onto `user._auth_methods`, and
`AuditService` folds it into every row the session writes (see [Audit Log](#audit-log) →
`extra_data.auth_methods`).

**Refresh and company switch keep them.** `POST /auth/refresh` and
`POST /auth/switch-company/{target_company_id}` copy the presented token's `amr` and `pst` into the
new tokens exactly, so a renewed badge session neither loses nor gains `"pin"`. A badge session's
`TOKEN_REFRESHED` row carries `extra_data.auth_methods`.

**A badge session ends when the PIN rule no longer backs it.** The answer is **401**
`{"code": "floor_pin_reauth_required", "message": "Sign in again with your badge and PIN."}` and
nothing is minted:

- **A `["badge", "pin"]` session is bound to the PIN it verified.** Once that PIN is reset (a new
  set time), cleared or cleared by a promotion, or when its token carries no usable `pst`, it is
  refused on **every request**, HTTP and WebSocket alike (`resolve_access_identity`; a WebSocket is
  closed with **1008** at its next identity check), and on refresh and company switch, which write a `TOKEN_REFRESH_FAILED` /
  `COMPANY_SWITCH_FAILED` row with `PIN changed`. So **setting a new PIN ends every badge + PIN
  session of that person at its next request**: that is the remedy for a leaked PIN. A PIN **lock**
  does not end a session that already proved the PIN.
- **A `["badge"]` session cannot outlive the rule.** Asking to refresh or switch company once its
  user **has** a PIN, needs a new one after a promotion, or the user's company **requires** one, it
  is refused with a `PIN now required` row. Its current access token (≤ 15 minutes) is not revoked;
  the session ends at its next refresh.
- A password session is never refused here.

The SPA treats this 401 on **any** request as the end of the session: it signs out without trying a
refresh and lands on the badge sign-in (the Login page opened on Badge Only, or the kiosk's badge
screen) with the server's message. Deactivating a user is **not** a substitute for a new PIN: it
only pauses a session, and once the account is reactivated its refresh tokens, still inside their
7-day window, work again.

**Sessions signed in before the deploy carry no `amr`.** Their refresh tokens have no claim to copy,
so they keep refreshing with none: their rows carry no `auth_methods`, and the reauth refusal cannot
recognize them as badge sessions, even with the policy on, until the person signs out and in again or
the session lapses (a solo kiosk logs out on idle; a crew-station token lasts 5 minutes). A desk
Employee-ID session that refreshes at least once a week never lapses, because every refresh restarts
its 7-day window, so it could outlive the policy indefinitely. Rotating `REFRESH_TOKEN_SECRET_KEY`
before turning the policy on for the first time ends all of them: every refresh token is refused
once, everyone signs in again, and the new badge sessions carry `amr` (see
[DEPLOYMENT.md → Floor PIN for badge sign-on](DEPLOYMENT.md#floor-pin-for-badge-sign-on-migration-130)).

## Core Endpoints

### Retired quote-nesting endpoints

Every `/api/v1/quote-nesting/*` route was removed with the Material Nesting estimator in
commit `3e17456e` (2026-09-16): the buyer material-plan PDF, catalog material resolution,
team drafts and their revisions, saved server calculations (including runtime readiness,
checkpoints and reports), spacing policies, and the original-DXF `/sources` attachments on
saved revisions. No router mounts that prefix any more, so a request to any of them returns
**404** (`backend/tests/api/test_quoting_cutover.py` pins it for the drafts, runs and
buyer-PDF paths). New estimates, including their
nesting, use `/fabrication-quotes` — see [FABRICATION_QUOTING.md](FABRICATION_QUOTING.md).

The tables those routes wrote (migrations `101`, `102`, `103` and `105`) are kept as
historical records; no route, service or job reads or writes them. Their database guards
are described in [SUPABASE_SECURITY.md](SUPABASE_SECURITY.md). Production laser nests
([Laser Nests](#laser-nests)) and the recorded-piece routes under `/inventory`
([Advisory physical-piece observations](#advisory-physical-piece-observations),
[Recorded-piece planning snapshot](#recorded-piece-planning-snapshot)) are separate and
unaffected.

### Global search and customer edits

`GET /search/` accepts `q` (1–100 characters), `types` (comma-separated entity
types), `offset` (0–100000) and `limit` (1–50, default 20). SQL ranks the entire
matching set before pagination: current exact matches, exact retired part aliases,
identifier prefixes, then broader matches. `total` and `categories` count the complete
selected result set; `has_more`, `offset` and `limit` describe its page. The full
results screen at `/search` retains query and type filters in the URL. Employee
directory results retain the existing Admin/Manager access restriction, and a **read-only API
token** never gets them, whatever its user's role: the Users tag is denied to read-only tokens, and
`user` results would expose names, emails and employee ids anyway.

Customer responses include every editable contact, address, payment, shipping and
note field. The customer editor sends only changed fields; an omitted field is
preserved, and an explicit blank clears a field where the schema permits it.
Updates record old/new values through the normal committed audit path.
Editing a soft-deleted customer returns 404; the update endpoint cannot reactivate
a deleted record. Customer pickers independently exclude tombstoned rows.

### Customers

`app/api/endpoints/customers.py`, mounted at `/customers`. Every route resolves the customer in the
active company; another company's customer id answers **404** with the same detail a missing id gets.

| Method | Endpoint | Description | Auth Required |
|--------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| GET | `/customers/` | List customers by name (`active_only` default `true`; `search` matches name, code, contact name, city; `include_deleted` is honored for Admin only; `limit` 1–5000, `offset`) | Yes |
| GET | `/customers/names` | `{id, name}` pairs of active, non-deleted customers, for pickers | Yes |
| GET | `/customers/{id}` | Customer detail | Yes |
| GET | `/customers/{id}/stats` | Parts and assemblies filed under the customer's name, work-order counts by status, and current / past / recent work orders, **from the active company only** (see note) | Yes |
| POST | `/customers/` | Create. `code` is optional and generated from the name when omitted. **400** `Customer name already exists` / `Customer code already exists` on a duplicate **within the company**. Writes an audit `CREATE` row in the same transaction | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| PUT | `/customers/{id}` | Partial update of a live customer (**404** on a soft-deleted one). A rename onto a name already used in the company is **400** `Customer name already exists`, including when a concurrent rename races past the check. `code` is not updatable. A **rename** writes its audit `UPDATE` row as required evidence: if the row cannot be written, **503** `The audit record for this customer rename could not be saved; nothing was changed. Retry.` and nothing is saved (export control reads a controlled customer's former names from these rows; see [EXPORT_CONTROL_AI_EGRESS.md](EXPORT_CONTROL_AI_EGRESS.md)). Other edits keep a best-effort audit row | Admin / Manager |
| DELETE | `/customers/{id}` | Soft delete by default (also clears `is_active`). A second soft delete of an already-deleted customer is **400** `Customer is already deleted` and changes nothing. `hard_delete=true` removes the row (a soft-deleted one too), and is refused **400** while parts of the active company carry the customer's name, **400** while a CAR names the customer (`Cannot hard delete: Customer is named on N corrective action report(s); soft delete it instead`), **400** `Cannot hard delete: Customer owns 2 inventory stock rows, 1 tool and 3 PO receipts recorded as customer property. …` (naming whichever counts apply) while any stock row, tool or PO receipt of the active company names the customer as its owner (migration `129`; any quantity, active or not, a voided receipt included). The remedy sentence depends on what blocks: when every blocker can be re-owned it reads `Change their ownership first (POST /inventory/items/{id}/ownership for stock, PUT /tool-management/tools/{id} for tools), or soft delete the customer.`; when a PO receipt, or a deactivated or empty stock row, blocks (none of which can be re-owned) it says to soft delete the customer instead, which keeps them naming their owner, and **400** `Cannot hard delete: Customer has export-control contracts or handling instructions. Soft delete it instead.` while any contract or handling instruction names the customer | Admin / Manager |
| POST | `/customers/{id}/restore` | Restore a soft-deleted customer (**400** if it is not deleted). Restore always sets `is_active = true` (see note) | Admin / Manager |
| POST | `/customers/import-csv` | See [Bulk Imports & Templates](#bulk-imports--templates-excel-migration-kit) | Admin / Manager |
| GET | `/customers/{id}/export-control` | The customer's export-control standing: `controlled` (derived from **every** contract and classified handling instruction it has ever had), `data_classification` (`itar_export_controlled` outranks `cui`), `controlling_contract_id`, `customer_is_deleted`, and every contract with its own `controlling` flag. A soft-deleted customer is readable | Admin (never an API token) |
| POST | `/customers/{id}/contracts` | Add a contract. Body: `contract_name` (required), `contract_number`, `itar_controlled`, `export_controlled`, `contains_cui`, `default_data_classification` (default `internal`), `effective_date`, `expiration_date`, `active` (default `true`), `handling_instructions`, and a required `reason` (1–1000 chars); unknown keys **422**. → **201** with the export-control view. Duplicate `contract_number` in the company → **409** | Admin (never an API token) |
| PUT | `/customers/{id}/contracts/{contract_id}` | Change the supplied fields of one of the customer's contracts; `reason` always required; an explicit `null` on a flag, `active`, the classification or `contract_name` is **422**. Not this customer's contract in this company → **404**; duplicate `contract_number` → **409**. A request that changes nothing writes nothing. There is no delete: un-marking is this `PUT` with the flags off | Admin (never an API token) |

> **Export control (Claude-plugin brief P0.3; owner decision 2026-11-13).** These three routes are
> the only writer of `customer_contracts`. A customer is **export-controlled** when any of its
> contracts has `itar_controlled`, `export_controlled` or `contains_cui` set, or is classified
> `itar_export_controlled` / `cui`. Every contract counts, whatever its `active` flag or dates,
> because ITAR obligations outlive the contract. An AI-external API token then sees that
> customer's work orders, parts, NCRs, quotes and purchasing records redacted
> ([docs/EXPORT_CONTROL_AI_EGRESS.md](EXPORT_CONTROL_AI_EGRESS.md)).
>
> Only an **Admin** may read or change it. A non-Admin gets **403** `Insufficient permissions`.
> **Any** API token, whatever its role or scope, gets **403** `"An API token cannot read or change
> a customer's export control: an Admin does it, signed in to the app."`. Writes run inside
> `required_audit`: a REQUIRED `customer_contract` CREATE / UPDATE row carries the `reason` and the
> customer's controlled state before and after. When the customer's standing changes (controlled ↔
> not, or ITAR ↔ CUI) the write also adds a `customer` `STATUS_CHANGE` row. If the audit cannot be
> written the answer is **503** `"The audit record for this export-control change could not be
> saved; nothing was changed. Retry."` and nothing is saved. Dates are stored as naive UTC.
> Another company's customer is **404**. A soft-deleted customer stays readable and markable,
> because its historical records stay controlled. The UI is the **Export control** panel on the
> customer detail in **Customers**, shown to Admins only. The two writes are **not MCP tools**
> (`catalog.EXCLUDED_OPERATIONS`), so not even a person's own JWT reaches them through an agent;
> `get_customer_export_control` stays a tool.

> **Create and update are now role-gated.** Both previously required only an authenticated user.
> Update is Admin / Manager, matching the rest of the customer master's writes (import, delete,
> restore) and the vendor master's create / update. Create is Admin / Manager / Supervisor, the same
> roles `POST /work-orders/` admits, because New Work Order creates the customer inline when the
> typed name is new and abandons the work-order submit if that create is refused. Other roles get
> **403** `Insufficient permissions`; reads stay open to every role. The Customers page does not yet
> hide Add / Edit by role, so a refused save reaches the user as an error toast. See
> [RBAC → Customers](RBAC_PERMISSIONS.md#customers).

> **Name and code are unique per company, not globally (migration `115`).** `create_all` had built
> `customers.name` and `customers.code` as global unique indexes, so one company's customer name or
> code blocked every other company from using it, and the refusal disclosed that it existed. A
> second company's generated `ACM001` was a **500**. Uniqueness is now
> `UNIQUE (company_id, name)` and `UNIQUE (company_id, code)`. Neither has a partial predicate, so a
> soft-deleted customer keeps its name and code: creating or renaming onto a tombstone's name or code
> is still **400**. A generated code is the first three letters or digits of the name plus a
> three-digit number, counted within the active company only, and it steps past any code already
> taken there, including a hand-keyed or soft-deleted one. A concurrent create that slips past the
> duplicate check is mapped to **400** `Customer name or code already exists`, and a concurrent
> rename to **400** `Customer name already exists`. Neither leaves a row change or an audit row.

> **`/stats` and the hard-delete check are tenant-scoped.** A customer's parts and work orders are
> linked by the free-text `customer_name`, not a foreign key. Both reads previously had no company
> predicate, so a name shared by two companies returned the other company's part numbers,
> work-order numbers and customer POs, and the hard-delete count refused the delete over the other
> company's parts while disclosing how many it had. Both now read the active company only.
>
> The hard-delete check counts parts, CARs (`cars.customer_id`, migration `122`) and owned stock rows,
> tools and PO receipts (`owner_customer_id`, migration `129`) only. Customer
> complaints, RMAs, RFQ quotes, fabrication
> quotes and the governance tables reference `customers.id` with no `ON DELETE`, so on PostgreSQL a
> hard delete of a customer they still reference fails with a database error (**500**) rather than
> a 400. Work orders that name the customer are not counted. Soft delete is unaffected.

> **Audit rows.** Create writes a `CREATE` row (it wrote none before). Soft delete's `DELETE` row
> records `old_values` `{is_deleted: false, is_active: <prior value>}`; because a second soft delete
> is refused, that row cannot be overwritten by a later one claiming the customer was live. Restore's
> `RESTORE` row
> records both `is_deleted` and `is_active`, old and new. A hard delete's
> `DELETE` row carries the full removed record in `old_values`, which is the only copy left after
> the commit. Unlike vendor restore, customer restore does not put back the `is_active` value the
> customer had before the delete; that prior value is recorded only in the soft-delete audit row.

### Custom Fields

`app/api/endpoints/custom_fields.py`, mounted at `/custom-fields`. Definitions and values are both
company-scoped.

| Method | Endpoint | Description | Auth Required |
|--------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| GET | `/custom-fields/definitions` | List definitions (`entity_type` filter; `active_only` default `true`) | Yes |
| POST | `/custom-fields/definitions` | Create a definition (**400** when the `field_key` already exists for that entity type in the company). Writes an audit `CREATE` row | Admin / Manager |
| GET | `/custom-fields/definitions/{id}` | Definition detail | Yes |
| PUT | `/custom-fields/definitions/{id}` | Update a definition. Writes an audit `UPDATE` row with the supplied fields' old and new values | Admin / Manager |
| DELETE | `/custom-fields/definitions/{id}` | Deactivate a definition (`is_active = false`; no row is removed). Writes an audit `STATUS_CHANGE` row (`active` → `inactive`); deactivating an already-inactive definition returns 200 and records nothing | Admin |
| GET | `/custom-fields/values/{entity_type}/{entity_id}` | `{entity_type, entity_id, fields: {field_key: value}}` for one record. Values of deactivated definitions are omitted. Accepts a soft-deleted record | Yes |
| POST | `/custom-fields/values/{entity_type}/{entity_id}` | Body `{field_key, value}`. Creates or overwrites one value on a live record. **404** when the field is not an active definition of the company; **400** when the value does not fit the field type | Yes |
| POST | `/custom-fields/values/bulk` | Body `{entity_type, entity_id, values: {field_key: value}}`. Returns `results[]`, one `success` or `error` per key; an unknown field or an unparseable value is an `error` and the other keys still apply | Yes |
| DELETE | `/custom-fields/values/{entity_type}/{entity_id}/{field_key}` | Remove one value. Works on a deactivated definition's value. **404** when the field or the value does not exist in the company | Yes |

`entity_type` is one of `part`, `work_order`, `work_center`, `customer`, `supplier` (a vendor),
`inventory` (an `inventory_items` stock row) and `bom`. `entity_id` is that record's id.

> **The value routes are tenant-scoped (they were not).** Before this change the four `/values/*`
> routes took no company: they looked definitions up by `field_key` across every company, never
> checked that `entity_id` existed, and read, overwrote and deleted value rows by id alone. New value
> rows were also built without `company_id`, which is NOT NULL, so creating a value always failed
> with a **500**. Now:
>
> - The target record must exist **in the active company**, or the route answers **404**
>   (`<entity_type> <entity_id> not found`) and writes nothing; for bulk, nothing at all is written.
>   The GET accepts a soft-deleted record; every write and the DELETE require a live one.
> - The definition is resolved by company, `field_key` and `entity_type`. Another company's
>   definition with the same key is never used.
> - Value rows are read, overwritten and deleted only within the active company, and new rows carry
>   `company_id`.
> - Every create, overwrite and delete writes an audit row: `resource_type` `custom_field_value`,
>   identifier `<entity_type>:<entity_id>:<field_key>`, the value columns old and new, and
>   `extra_data` `{field_key, entity_type, entity_id}`. The delete stays physical (value rows carry
>   no soft delete), so its `DELETE` row records the removed value.
> - A value the field type cannot hold is **400** `Invalid value for '<field_key>' (<field_type>)`
>   instead of a 500. A `date` / `datetime` value must be an ISO-8601 string; a JSON number,
>   boolean, object or array is refused this way rather than failing at the database. In bulk only
>   parse errors become per-key `error` results; a database error now fails the whole request
>   instead of being reported as one key's error.
>
> **Definition writes are audited too.** Create, update and deactivate write `custom_field_definition`
> rows (identifier `<entity_type>:<field_key>`). Deactivating a definition hides every value under
> it, and editing one (`options`, `is_active`) changes how those values read, so who changed a
> definition is recorded alongside the value writes.
>
> **Known gap: the value routes have no role gate.** Any authenticated user of the company, Viewer
> included, can set or delete a value. That predates this change, is not intended policy, and is
> tracked as a follow-up. See [RBAC → Custom Fields](RBAC_PERMISSIONS.md#custom-fields).

### Work Orders

| Method | Endpoint | Description | Auth Required |
|--------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| GET | `/work-orders/` | List all work orders (`skip` ≥ 0, `limit` 1–5000 default 100 — the standard list tier, see [Pagination](#pagination)). `deleted_only=true` returns **only** this company's soft-deleted work orders — the restore view, **Admin / Manager**, and the only read in the API that can see one; see "Seeing a deleted work order" below | Yes (`deleted_only=true`: Admin / Manager) |
| GET | `/work-orders/browse` | **The bounded, server-filtered page behind the Work Orders list screen.** Returns an **envelope**, not a bare array. Query: `skip` ≥ 0 (default 0; a `skip` past the last page is clamped to that page's start, and the response's `skip` reports the clamped value), `limit` **1–100** (default 50); `status` (one `WorkOrderStatus`; omitted = every status except complete / closed / cancelled); `search` (≤ 200 chars, a **literal** case-insensitive substring — `%` / `_` are not wildcards — over WO number, customer name, customer PO, lot, unit #, part number and part name); `customer` (≤ 255, exact customer name); `hide_cots` (default `true`: hides work orders whose part is purchased / hardware / raw material; part-less ones stay); `scope` (`overdue` \| `due_today`, open work orders by `due_date` against the **Central** date; or `late`, the daily `wo.late` summary's own rule: a released / in-progress / on-hold work order past its promise date — `must_ship_by`, else `due_date` — drafts never late); `work_order_type` (`production` \| `laser_cutting`, unknown → **422**; `laser_cutting` = nest packages — standalone laser work orders and the laser children a nest import hangs off a production job); `sort` (`work_order_number` \| `part` \| `customer` \| `due_date` \| `priority` (default) \| `status`, nulls last, ID tiebreaker) with `direction` (`asc` default \| `desc`); `group` (`none` default \| `customer` \| `part` \| `status`, rows ordered by group first). Response: `items` (`WorkOrderSummary` rows with operation progress), `total` (the full filtered count), `skip`, `limit`, `has_next`, `stats` (`overdue` / `in_progress` / `due_today` over the filtered set), `customers` (distinct customer names under every filter **except** `customer` — it honors `work_order_type` — capped at 1000, with `customers_truncated`), `group_totals` (full counts for only the groups on this page; `{}` when `group=none`), and `type_counts` (`{production, laser_cutting}`, both always present, zero-filled: rows per type under every **other** filter, `customer` included, deliberately **ignoring** `work_order_type` so each type chip shows its own count). A pure read sent `Cache-Control: no-store`: it **never reconciles on read** — no completion evidence, READY promotion or inventory effect — so loading the list does not heal a stranded work order the way `GET /work-orders/{id}` does (see "A read heals a stranded work order" below) | Effective `work_orders:view` in the active company (every role by default; **403** when a company role override removes it) |
| POST | `/work-orders/` | Create work order. `work_order_type` is validated against the `WorkOrderType` vocabulary (**422** on an unknown value), and `'laser_cutting'` is **refused on create** (422) — nest-dispatch WOs are minted only by the laser nest import paths (see note below). Body accepts `sequential_operations` (**default `true`** — a sequenced routing; see "READY promotion" below) and the optional `unit_number` (≤ 50 chars — see "Unit #" below). Each supplied `operations[]` row accepts an optional `routing_operation_id` that keeps that routing step's process sheet; a link that is not on the part's released routing is **409** `ROUTING_OPERATION_UNMATCHED`, and a create that leaves a sheet-bearing step off the job is **503** (nothing saved) when its required audit row cannot be written — see "Process sheets on supplied operations" below | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| GET | `/work-orders/preview-operations/{part_id}` | The operations `POST /work-orders/` would copy from the part's released routing (query `quantity`, default 1). `operations_preview` rows carry `routing_operation_id`, the `sequence` / `operation_number` the routed create would assign, and `process_sheet_id` / `process_sheet_number` / `process_sheet_released` (`false` = creating from this routing would be **409** `PROCESS_SHEET_UNAVAILABLE`; `null` = no sheet). Rows are returned for every part type, not only parts with a BOM. **404** for a part outside the active company. Pure read. See "Process sheets on supplied operations" below | Yes |
| GET | `/work-orders/process-sheet-gaps` | **Quality's Sheet Gaps list** — live work orders whose part's released routing (or a BOM component's) carries process sheets but whose operations hold no snapshotted process-sheet step. Query `limit` 1–500 (default 200); response `{total, items}` with `total` counting every match. Pure read, writes nothing. MCP tool `list_process_sheet_gaps`. See "Process sheets on supplied operations" below | Admin / Manager / Quality |
| GET | `/work-orders/{id}` | Get work order by ID. Also carries the job's cost by element (`job_cost_actuals`), the inventory-ledger material figure (`issued_material_cost`) and, per operation, where its actual hours come from (`hours_source`, `recorded_setup_hours`, `recorded_run_hours`, `hours_include_backfill`) — see "Cost and actual hours on the work-order read" below | Yes |
| GET | `/work-orders/by-number/{wo_number}` | Get work order by number: the **same body** as by ID (every computed field included). A soft-deleted work order is **404**, as by ID. Unlike the read by ID it does **not** reconcile on read — it writes nothing | Yes |
| GET | `/work-orders/{id}/timeline` | Chronological job history with category, actor and time filters; opaque cursor, `limit` 1–100 (default 30). Returns business events and source links, not raw audit payloads. Each item a single operation owns (its start / finish, production receipts, process-step evidence, labor, a blocker filed against it) carries `operation_id`; the job's own items carry `null` | Yes |
| PUT | `/work-orders/{id}` | Update work order (an absent, other-company **or soft-deleted** work order is **404** `Work order not found` — restore is its own verb; body requires the WO's current `version` — stale → 409; also 409 if it moves a terminal WO back to a non-terminal status, **or sets `status` to COMPLETE/CLOSED from any status other than COMPLETE/CLOSED** — see "Terminal-state lock" below). **`due_date` is the one non-`status` field that IS status-gated: changing it on a COMPLETE/CLOSED/CANCELLED work order returns 409** (see "Due date on a finished job" below). Other non-`status` fields such as `notes` / `special_instructions` / `unit_number` carry **no status gate**: they are editable at any status, including terminal ones (send `unit_number: null` — or `""`, which is trimmed to NULL — to clear it). **The flip verb for `sequential_operations`** — turning it *on* returns **409** on a laser nest WO, and **409 naming the operations** when work is already under way out of sequence; otherwise it demotes un-worked blocked operations READY → PENDING, one audit row each (see "READY promotion" below). **`status: on_hold` on a DRAFT work order returns 409** (a draft has nothing on the floor to hold — release it first); this `PUT` is the "Hold Work Order" write for a released / in-progress job, and the door that puts a held job back on the floor is `POST /work-orders/{id}/resume` (this `PUT` can still move a held job to `draft` or `cancelled`, which keeps it off the floor; its blind move to `released` / `in_progress` is a known gap — see "Draft and on-hold work orders refuse every start" below). **Any move to `draft`** (from released / in progress / on hold) returns every un-worked READY operation — laser nests included — to PENDING with one **required** audit row each; **503**, nothing changed, when those rows cannot be written (see "Returning a job to draft" below). **Lowering `quantity_ordered` below what a whole-order operation has already accounted for (its good + scrap) returns 409** naming the operation, before any field is written — lower the order only by units no operation has started; **raising** it once a whole-order or component operation has completed returns 409 too; whole-order targets restated as `component_quantity` move with the order (audited); an API token lowering it once work is recorded gets 403, as does an API token raising the header's `quantity_scrapped` (only a person declares scrap — owner decision 2026-11-07), changing `scrap_reason`, or changing the header's `quantity_complete` / `quantity_scrapped` in either direction (this PR's extension); and a `sequential_operations` flip that would re-interpret a declared short returns 409 (see "Short count at completion" below) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| DELETE | `/work-orders/{id}` | Delete work order (soft by default; `hard_delete=true` only for draft/cancelled, and refused **409** when ledger-backed ties or saved templates reference it, or when it has comments) | Admin / Manager |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/restore` | Restore a soft-deleted work order (**400** if it is not deleted). Re-opens the ties the delete cancelled — **except** any whose part has since been reclassified into one the shop produces. Returns an **envelope** (`message` + `skipped_material_allocations`), not a bare message; see "Restoring a work order" below. Reached from Work Orders → **Deleted** (`deleted_only=true` above) | Admin / Manager |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/release` | Release to production. **400** `Only draft work orders can be released` when not DRAFT, **400** `Work order must have at least one operation` when it has none — the only two checks; there is no material, blocker or readiness gate (see "Releasing work orders" below). **404** when missing or soft-deleted | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/work-orders/bulk-release` | **Release several DRAFT work orders in one call.** Body `{"work_order_ids": [...]}`: 1–50 positive ids (repeats count toward the 50 and are de-duplicated, first occurrence kept); any other key → **422**. Each id is judged and released exactly as `POST /work-orders/{id}/release` would, all in **one** commit. **200** once the body validates — even when every item was refused — with `{results, released_count, error_count}`, one result per distinct id in request order, unless the whole request fails after the per-item phase (the audit rows or the commit: **409** on a lost lock race, otherwise 5xx, nothing saved). Not an MCP tool. See "Releasing several work orders at once" below | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/start` | Start production: a **RELEASED** work order → IN_PROGRESS. **409** on a DRAFT (release first) or ON_HOLD (resume it — this verb no longer lifts a hold) work order, **400** on any other non-released status, **404** when missing or soft-deleted, **409** on a concurrent write | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/resume` | **Resume Work Order** — lift a *work-order* hold. Never releases: the target comes from the release record (`released_at` / `released_by`) — IN_PROGRESS when released and worked, RELEASED when released and unworked, **DRAFT** when no release is on record (un-worked READY operations, laser nests included, return to PENDING). **400** when not on hold, **404** when missing or soft-deleted, **503** (nothing changed) when the required audit rows cannot be written. Operation-level holds are untouched. See "Draft and on-hold work orders refuse every start" below | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/complete` | Force-complete a work order (privileged override), booking `quantity_complete` as its finished count — the header is **set** to it. **409** if the WO is CANCELLED or an open operation is on hold. **403** for an API token sending a `quantity_scrapped` above the header's recorded scrap (owner decision 2026-11-07: only a person declares scrap), and first among the quantity refusals for an API token completing short or above what the floor recorded. **409** when `quantity_complete` exceeds what the floor recorded (naming the binding operation) unless `quantity_override_reason` is sent, and **400** above what can still exist once declared shorts and covered scrap are out, even with a reason; **409** when the shortfall below the order is not covered by floor-reported scrap or `quantity_scrapped` (with a reason); **503** (nothing saved) when the required audit row cannot be written. See "Short count at completion" below | Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Quality |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/duplicate` | **Duplicate a work order** — copy its *plan* (operations, laser nests, open material ties, re-snapshotted process-sheet steps) onto a new **DRAFT** WO. Body `{quantity_ordered, due_date}`; **201** returning an **envelope**, not a bare work order. See "Duplicating a work order" below | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/operations` | Add an operation to a work order | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| PUT | `/work-orders/operations/{id}` | Update an operation (body now also accepts `work_center_id` — move the operation to another work center; see note below). **409** if it sets `status` to COMPLETE on a not-yet-complete operation — completion goes through the completion endpoints (see "Terminal-state lock"). **409** with the start gate's text if it sets `status` to IN_PROGRESS on an operation of a draft, on-hold or complete / closed / cancelled work order, and **409** "release first" if it sets `status` to READY on a draft — both before any field is written; re-sending the operation's current status is not a transition. **409** with the same text when it **raises** `quantity_complete` on an operation that is (or this write leaves) PENDING / READY of a draft or on-hold work order. These start-gate refusals answer **before** the open-operation count 409s below, so a not-started operation of a draft or held job always gets "release first" / "Resume Work Order", never a count text naming doors that job keeps shut. **404** `Work order not found` when the operation's work order is soft-deleted (see "Draft and on-hold work orders refuse every start"). **On a COMPLETE operation, changing `quantity_complete` or `status`, or lowering `quantity_scrapped`, returns 409** — those are the completion record; correct the good count with `…/reduce-production`, which can reopen the operation (re-sending the stored values, and every other field, is still accepted; scrap found after the close may be **added** with a reason, as required audit evidence, but only into units still unaccounted — a rise past that is 409). On an open operation, raising `quantity_complete` above the good ceiling or the floor's labor record returns 409; an API token may not change the counts or the scrap reason (403 — a `quantity_scrapped` rise or a reason change gets the scrap text, owner decision 2026-11-07). See "Short count at completion". **`inspection_complete` is not an updatable field:** a body that contains the key, with any value (`true`, `false`, `null`), is refused **422** (`inspection_complete cannot be set by an operation update. Sign off the inspection with POST /api/v1/shop-floor/operations/{operation_id}/inspection, which records who signed and when.`) rather than silently ignored — the sign-off verb is the flag's only writer (Shop Floor → "Inspection Schema"). `requires_inspection` is still accepted, and setting it signs nothing | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/work-orders/operations/{id}/start` | Start an operation (**office** verb — operators start work through `PUT /shop-floor/operations/{id}/start` and the kiosk, which stay operator-open). Refused before any write, in the shop-floor twin's order: **400** already complete / already in progress (it never re-opens or re-stamps one), **404** work order missing or soft-deleted, **409** draft / on-hold / terminal work order, **409** operation on hold (starting does not lift a hold), **400** predecessors | Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Quality |
| POST | `/work-orders/operations/{id}/complete` | Record an operation's good and scrap **totals** from the office. It **closes only when good + scrap cover every unit that reached the operation**; otherwise it saves progress and stays open (a submit that changes nothing is a **200** "No change" that writes nothing). 409 if the parent WO is terminal; **409 for a READY operation on a draft or on-hold WO** — completing it would start it. Query params `quantity_scrapped` (a total that never lowers), `scrap_reason` / `scrap_reason_code_id`, `quantity_override_reason`, `acknowledge_open_entries` — see "Short count at completion" below. **403** for an API token raising the scrap total (owner decision 2026-11-07: only a person declares scrap). **Office** verb — the shop-floor twin is the operator path | Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Quality |
| POST | `/work-orders/operations/{id}/reduce-production` | Supervisor/office over-count correction — walk back good-count across **any** operator's **unapproved** labor on the operation (an operation nobody ever clocked in to has its desk-entered good lowered directly, up to that count); **a COMPLETE operation is correctable here** (unlike the operator's twin), a terminal WO is not; no clock-in required. A correction that would leave a COMPLETE operation short is **409** unless the body sends `reopen_operation: true`, which returns it to in progress (see note below). A standing API token is **403** on every correction | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| GET | `/work-orders/{id}/material-allocations` | List the work order's material ties (`include_inactive`, default `true`) | Yes |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/material-allocations` | Tie a material part to the work order or one of its operations (**201**) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| PATCH | `/work-orders/{id}/material-allocations/{allocation_id}` | Edit an **open** tie's quantities, lot pin, or notes | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| DELETE | `/work-orders/{id}/material-allocations/{allocation_id}` | Untie (status → `cancelled`; the row is never physically deleted) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| GET | `/work-orders/{id}/material-allocations/{allocation_id}/consumption` | Per-source-lot ledger position of a tie (`issued` / `returned` / `net`) — the pre-confirm read behind the return dialog | Yes |
| POST | `/work-orders/{id}/material-allocations/{allocation_id}/return` | **Return consumed material to its source lots** — reasoned, audited, compensating. The only verb on this router that posts inventory | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| GET | `/work-orders/{id}/backflush-preview` | **Dry run (PR 4.5)** — what completing this work order would consume, per component and per lot, before anything moves. Pure read: no ledger row, no audit row, no event | Yes |

> **Comments on a work order** (the detail page's Comments panel, with @mentions and a Watch
> toggle) are their own routes, `/comments` and `/watchers` with `entity_type=work_order` — see
> [Comments and watchers](#comments-and-watchers).

> **Tenant isolation on operation/completion endpoints.** The operation- and completion-level
> endpoints above (`/start`, `/complete`, `/operations/{id}`, `/operations/{id}/start`,
> `/operations/{id}/complete`, `/operations`) and their shop-floor counterparts (see below) scope
> every work-order / operation lookup to the caller's **active company** (`get_current_company_id`).
> An id belonging to another tenant returns **404 before any mutation** (not 403, so a guessed id
> can't be used to drive another company's operation or work order). State transitions on these
> paths — operation/WO **start** and **complete**, manual `/work-orders/{id}/complete` (status +
> the quantities it sets), and shipment-close — are recorded in the tamper-evident audit trail
> (`GET /audit/`) in addition to the existing real-time operational events.
>
> **Concurrency on completion endpoints.** Operation/work-order **start** and **complete**
> (`/operations/{id}/start`, `/operations/{id}/complete`, `/operations/{id}` update, and
> `/work-orders/{id}/complete`) now enforce optimistic locking on the underlying operation / work
> order row. A concurrent stale update returns **409 Conflict**
> (`{"detail": "This … was modified concurrently. Refresh and retry…"}`) instead of silently losing
> the update; the client should re-fetch and retry. The server also takes a row lock
> (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`) around the over-completion check so two simultaneous completions cannot
> double-count quantity.
>
> **Optimistic locking on the work-order header (`PUT /work-orders/{id}`).** The update body's
> required `version` is enforced: it must equal the work order's current `version` (returned on every
> work-order response) or the update is rejected with **409 Conflict**
> (`{"detail": "Work order was modified by someone else. Refresh and try again."}`) before any field
> is written. On 409 the client should re-fetch the WO (picking up the fresh `version`) and retry.
> `version` is never client-writable — a successful update increments it server-side (SQLAlchemy
> `version_id_col` on `WorkOrder`), and responses carry the real counter. Beyond this endpoint, the
> mapping makes **every** WorkOrder write path conflict-checked: a genuinely concurrent stale write on
> any other path (priority updates, kiosk status flips, soft delete) surfaces as **409 Conflict**
> (`{"detail": "This record was modified by someone else. Refresh and try again."}`) via an app-wide
> `StaleDataError` handler instead of silently losing the write.
>
> **`version` is carried on the LIST shape too** (`WorkOrderSummary`, so every `GET /work-orders/` row
> has it), not only on the detail response. That is what lets a client edit a header field straight
> from a list row without first round-tripping `GET /work-orders/{id}` — which is **not** a plain read:
> it runs the operation-quantity reconcile and can COMMIT writes against the work order. The summary is
> built kwarg-by-kwarg, so the field must be populated explicitly; omitted, every row would ship the
> schema default `0` and every edit from a list would 409.
>
> **A version fetched into a list is a WEAK guard, and a client editing from one needs a second.** The
> lock stops a write that landed between the read and the `PUT`, but a list that polls (the app's
> work-order list refreshes every 30s, on window focus, and on every work-order broadcast) silently
> refreshes `version` under an open editor, so the 409 never fires and a concurrent edit is overwritten
> with a clean 200. Any inline editor on a refreshing list must therefore ALSO hold its own
> before/after baseline of the field it edits and confirm before overwriting a changed value — see
> `frontend/src/pages/WorkOrders.tsx` (inline due-date edit) and the same guard on `WorkOrderDetail`.
>
> **Due date on a finished job — 409.** Changing `due_date` on a work order in a terminal status
> (COMPLETE / CLOSED / CANCELLED) is refused:
> `{"detail": "cannot change the due date of a work order in terminal status 'complete': its due date is
> the promise date its delivery performance was scored against."}`. OTD scores against
> `coalesce(must_ship_by, due_date)`, so moving that date after the fact silently rewrites a delivery
> result that is already recorded — and afterwards the rewrite is indistinguishable from the job having
> always been due then.
>
> The guard is deliberately narrow in three ways. It refuses only the `due_date` **component**, not the
> whole request, so `notes` / `special_instructions` / `unit_number` stay editable at any status (a
> correction written after the fact is what those fields are for). It refuses only an actual **change**,
> so re-sending the value a terminal WO already carries is idempotent — a client echoing back a whole
> record does not 409. And it runs **before the first `setattr`**, so a refused request leaves every
> field untouched.
>
> This is the **server-side** enforcement, added because the rule previously lived only in one UI: the
> work-order list hid the control while the detail page and the API permitted the same edit, which made
> the audit trail look like a restriction was holding when two other doors were open. Both UI surfaces
> now hide the due-date pencil on a terminal WO to match, but the 409 is what enforces it.
>
> The rule is **one implementation**, `services/work_order_due_date.py`
> (`assert_due_date_change_allowed`), shared by this `PUT` and Hank's `change_due_date` task (Hank →
> "Reviewed task contract"), so the two doors cannot drift apart. The `PUT` only judges the change
> there; its own `setattr` loop still writes the value.
>
> **READY promotion: a sequenced ROUTING or a DISPATCH POOL, chosen per work order.** Which of the two
> a work order is, is its own setting — `sequential_operations`, added by migration `081` and carried on
> the create body, the update body, and every work-order response and summary.
> - **`true` — a sequenced ROUTING.** An operation reaches READY only once **every** lower-sequence
>   operation of that work order is COMPLETE, **its own work center included**. The motivating case:
>   WO-20260807-006 is a 4-operation weld assembly (10 Skid Fit → 20 Wall Fit Up → 30 Accessory Fit Up →
>   40 Weld Out) whose first three operations sit on one weld cell, so the pooled rule unlocked all three
>   at once and the build order was lost on the floor.
> - **`false` — a DISPATCH POOL.** Operations sharing a work center do **not** block each other: they
>   promote together and are mutually startable. This is the pre-`081` rule unchanged — a batch WO
>   carrying ~18 press-brake items as one operation each on one machine shows all 18, where a
>   lowest-sequence-only rule showed 1 (the board and kiosk surface READY work **only**).
>
> **The create default and the backfill default are deliberately opposite.** The column's
> `server_default` is `false`, so every work order that already existed when `081` ran backfilled to
> **pooled** — exactly what it was released and scheduled under, so no in-flight job changed rules
> underneath the floor. The **create** default is `true`, so every work order minted from here on is a
> **sequenced routing** (the common case, and the one the pooled rule got wrong). The migration carries
> no backfill pass and no `UPDATE`: converting an existing job is an explicit, audited flip through
> `PUT /work-orders/{id}` (below). The column is `NOT NULL`, so the field is always present on a
> response — a client never has to interpret an absent value.
>
> **Cross-work-center ordering is preserved either way**, and the two modes are **indistinguishable on a
> conventional routing** whose steps each sit at a *different* work center — the same-work-center
> question never arises, at most one operation can pass the gate, and exactly one goes READY under
> either setting.
>
> **One rule, four seams, and the action gates read the same setting.** Promotion is a single
> implementation (`promote_ready_operations`) reached from **four** places — `POST
> /work-orders/{id}/release`; the shared finalizer after each operation completion that leaves work
> remaining (so it also covers the shop-floor and reconcile-on-read completion paths); the **read path**
> (see "A read heals a stranded work order" below); and `PUT /shop-floor/operations/{id}/resume`, which
> lands the resumed operation at PENDING and delegates any lift back to READY to this same rule. Each
> resolves the work order's mode **once per call**, and none of the four promotes a **DRAFT** or
> terminal work order: the rule itself returns nothing for one (see "DRAFT is never promoted by a read
> — or by anything else" below). The predecessor gate behind every *action* —
> `operation_action_gates.operation_blocked_by_predecessors`, used by `POST /shop-floor/clock-in`, both
> office verbs, both shop-floor verbs, the queue's check-in-state read, and `POST
> /scanner/resolve-action` — resolves it from the **same** function on the **same** work order. So an
> operation a sequenced routing keeps off the dispatch board is also **refused by a badge scan**, and an
> operation a badge can start is visible. Don't read the flag anywhere else: two readings is exactly how
> the office and floor rules drifted apart the first time.
>
> **Unresolvable → pooled.** `work_order_allows_same_work_center` returns *pooled* whenever it cannot
> read the flag (a null work order, a row or stub predating the column) — the pre-`081` value every
> caller used to hard-code. An unresolvable work order can therefore never silently **tighten** a gate
> and strand work the floor was already allowed to start.
>
> **Laser WOs ignore the setting entirely.** `is_laser_dispatch_work_order` short-circuits **above** it
> at every seam and is **strictly fuller** — it drops predecessor gating altogether, so nests promote
> across two lasers and a **held nest does not block its siblings**. It must not be collapsed into the
> same-work-center allowance. Both laser work-order constructors pin `sequential_operations=false` so a
> nest package never serializes a claim its own behavior contradicts, and `PUT /work-orders/{id}`
> returns **409** on an attempt to set it `true` on one.
>
> **The bulk loader now agrees rather than diverging.** `POST /work-orders/import` still carries its own
> inline "promote **exactly one** operation" release rule, and it does not pin the flag — so an imported
> work order takes the sequenced create default and the read-path seam converges it onto the
> **sequenced** rule, which promotes exactly the one operation the loader already promoted. (Under the
> pooled rule the first reconciling read promoted the rest of the pool instead.)
>
> **Flipping the setting — `PUT /work-orders/{id}`.** Roles **Admin / Manager / Supervisor**. The body
> already requires the work order's current `version` (stale → **409** before any field is written), and
> `sequential_operations` is optional, so an update that never mentions it never changes it. Two further
> **409**s are specific to turning it **ON** (`false` → `true`), and both are raised **before the first
> field is written**, so a refused flip leaves the row untouched:
> - **A laser nest work order** — `{"detail": "cannot switch a laser nest work order to sequential
>   operations: its nests are a dispatch pool and are deliberately startable in any order."}`
> - **Work already under way out of sequence** — if any operation the strict rule would block has been
>   worked (status IN_PROGRESS, an `actual_start`, booked good or scrapped quantity, or **any**
>   `TimeEntry` against it, open or closed), the flip is refused and the detail **names** the operations
>   (`OP{sequence} {name}`). The reason is not tidiness: every completion verb re-evaluates the
>   predecessor gate at action time, so an operation being worked ahead of its predecessors would become
>   **uncompletable** the instant the flag flipped, and nothing would heal it (promotion only ever moves
>   forward). Complete those operations — or the earlier ones they run ahead of — then flip.
>
> On a successful **ON** flip the endpoint also **demotes** the un-worked operations the pooled rule had
> already promoted: READY → PENDING, one `audit_log` **status-change** row per operation
> (`extra_data.transition = "sequential_operations_enabled"`), and the count on the `work_order_updated`
> event payload as `operations_returned_to_pending`. It is one of the callers of the **one** rule
> that moves an operation backwards (`work_order_state_service.demote_ready_operations` — four
> callers, three scopes: this flip is `sequencing`; `POST /work-orders/{id}/resume` landing a held
> job at DRAFT and this same `PUT` moving a job to `status: draft` are both `all_unworked`; the office
> reduce-production `reopen_operation` (`reopen_completed_operation`) is `blocked_by`, demoting only
> the un-worked READY operations the reopened one now blocks, audited
> `extra_data.transition = "predecessor_reopened"`. Holds and operation resume are actor decisions
> about one operation, and unschedule's READY → PENDING is transient), and it exists because
> promotion is forward-only: without it, turning the setting on would fix only the *next*
> work order, never the one being looked at. It never touches a worked operation, and it only demotes
> what the new rule actually blocks — so the lowest startable operation stays READY and the floor is
> never left with a work order it cannot start at all.
>
> **Turning it OFF needs no sweep.** `true` → `false` is repaired by the read-path heal, which
> re-promotes the pool on the next reconciling read.
>
> **A cleared blocker lands at PENDING on a sequenced routing.** When the last open blocker on a held
> operation clears, an operation that was **already started** (`actual_start`) returns to IN_PROGRESS as
> before; an **un-started** operation whose predecessors are still open now lands at **PENDING**, not
> READY. READY would put a card on the dispatch board and the kiosk that every start verb refuses, and
> nothing would heal it (the read-path heal reads PENDING rows only). Unchanged for a pooled work order
> and for a laser nest, where the shared gate short-circuits to "not blocked".
>
> **Duplicating a work order carries the setting.** `sequential_operations` is *plan*, not production
> record, so `POST /work-orders/{id}/duplicate` copies it **explicitly** rather than letting the new row
> take the create default — which is the *opposite* value for a pooled source, so a duplicated
> batch/pool WO would otherwise come back as a sequenced routing and show the floor one item of eighteen.
>
> **What this setting is NOT: an airtight enforcement control.** It governs what reaches READY and what
> the *action* verbs refuse. **Four write paths still reach COMPLETE or READY with no predecessor
> check**, so a sequenced routing constrains the normal flow without making out-of-order completion
> unreachable. Stated plainly so nobody plans around a guarantee that isn't there:
> - **`_sync_operation_status_from_quantity`** (read path) flips an operation to COMPLETE from closed
>   labor evidence once its booked good count reaches the units that reached it (the target, unless an
>   upstream close in its chain declared a short — see "Short count at completion") — ungated by
>   sequence. Scrap never counts there, so a read never closes a short.
> - **`_copy_slot_completion_evidence`** (read path) flips regenerated sibling rows sharing a progress
>   key to COMPLETE from a completed sibling's evidence — ungated by sequence.
> - **`POST /work-orders/{id}/complete`** (Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Quality) force-completes every
>   still-open operation through the shared finalizer — ungated by sequence. (It *does* refuse **409**
>   when an open operation is ON_HOLD.)
> - **`PUT /work-orders/operations/{id}`** (Admin / Manager / Supervisor) carries no predecessor
>   check; a supervisor may hand-set an operation to **READY** through its blind `setattr` loop on a
>   released, in-progress or on-hold work order. That is a **deliberate, role-gated, audited supervisor
>   override** — the full old→new row diff lands on the tamper-evident chain — and the read-path heal
>   will **never re-demote** it, because that heal reads PENDING rows only. (Its status refusals are
>   work-order-state rules, not sequence rules: COMPLETE always, IN_PROGRESS on a draft / on-hold /
>   terminal work order, READY on a draft — see "Draft and on-hold work orders refuse every start" —
>   and any status change at all on an operation that is already COMPLETE — see "Short count at
>   completion".)
>
> **`_apply_work_order_schedule` promotes without a gate and is provably safe — don't "fix" it.**
> `PUT /scheduling/work-orders/{id}/schedule`, `…/schedule-earliest`, and
> `POST /scheduling/bulk-schedule-earliest` each promote `current_op` PENDING → READY on a RELEASED /
> IN_PROGRESS work order with no predecessor check. `current_op` comes from `_get_current_operation`,
> which is *operations sorted by sequence → the first one that is not COMPLETE*. Every lower-sequence
> operation of that candidate is therefore COMPLETE by construction, and the strict rule blocks an
> operation only when some lower-sequence operation is **not** COMPLETE — so the sequenced rule can never
> block the one operation this path promotes. Adding a gate here would change no behavior and would
> create a fifth copy of the rule.
>
> **A read heals a stranded work order.** The release and completion seams above cannot reach a work
> order that was **already RELEASED** before the pooled rule shipped: `POST /work-orders/{id}/release`
> refuses anything that is not DRAFT, so such a WO kept the one-at-a-time promotion it was released
> under and its operations 2..N sat PENDING indefinitely — invisible to the kiosk and the dispatch
> board, which surface READY work only. The reconcile-on-read pass
> (`reconcile_work_orders_from_completion_evidence`) now re-runs the **same** promotion last, after
> the completion evidence has landed, so a stranded work order repairs itself the next time anyone
> loads it. No new endpoint, no data migration, no owner action.
> - **Which reads heal.** `GET /work-orders`, `GET /work-orders/{id}`, `GET /shop-floor/dashboard`
>   (bounded to the most-recently-touched open WOs by `SHOP_FLOOR_DASHBOARD_RECONCILE_LIMIT`, and only
>   on a **200**: its `ETag` **304** returns before the reconcile, which a cross-origin SPA now
>   actually receives — see [CORS](#cors)),
>   `GET /shop-floor/operations`, and `GET /shop-floor/operations/{id}`. `POST /work-orders/` also
>   reconciles, but a brand-new WO is DRAFT, so the DRAFT carve-out below makes it the no-op it has
>   always been — **six** handlers call the reconcile, five of which can actually promote.
> - **This is also what converges a work order onto a *changed* `sequential_operations` setting.**
>   Turning the setting **off** leaves operations to be re-promoted by this heal; turning it **on**
>   demotes at the flip (above) and needs no read. Either way, **opening the work order — or a
>   shop-floor operations / dashboard read — is what converges it. Polling the dispatch board or the
>   kiosk queue will not**, because neither reconciles.
> - **Which do not.** The **kiosk queue and the dispatch-board / work-center-queue endpoints do not
>   reconcile.** Polling a board will not repair a stranded WO — **opening the work order, or a
>   shop-floor operations/dashboard read, is what repairs it**, after which the board shows the pool.
>   Because the operations list filters status in SQL, the load that heals is the one *before* the
>   rows appear: the operator's next poll shows them.
> - **DRAFT is never promoted by a read — or by anything else.** Release remains the authorization
>   step and the record of who authorized production, so a GET must not put unreleased work on the
>   floor's board. Since Wave 2 the carve-out lives in the promotion rule itself
>   (`promote_ready_operations` returns nothing for a DRAFT or terminal work order), so it holds at all
>   four seams: the completion seam no longer promotes on a draft either (finishing labor that was
>   running when a job was resumed to DRAFT used to put the operations the resume had just demoted
>   back on the board). A DRAFT WO promotes at `POST /work-orders/{id}/release` exactly as before —
>   Release writes RELEASED before it promotes — so the carve-out delays promotion to the authorized
>   moment, it does not lose it. Terminal WOs (COMPLETE / CLOSED / CANCELLED) are
>   likewise skipped, including one this same pass just drove to COMPLETE. Every other non-terminal
>   status promotes — a work order whose **header** is ON_HOLD included, matching what the completion
>   seam already does; the **operation**-level ON_HOLD carve-out is the one that stops a pool.
> - **The heal runs the rule, it does not relax it.** Cross-work-center ordering still holds, the
>   ON_HOLD carve-out below still blocks (a page load is not a way around a quality stop), only
>   PENDING rows are touched, and the write set is scoped to the work order's own company. It is
>   idempotent — a second read promotes nothing and emits no duplicate `operation_ready` event — and
>   best-effort per work order, so a failure on one cannot 500 a board load for the rest.
> - **Still unaudited, as at the other two seams.** PENDING → READY writes no `audit_log` row (READY
>   is queue state, not a production record); traceability for the flip is the tenant-scoped
>   `operation_ready` OperationalEvent, which is what the Lean queue-time metric reads.
>
> **A failed reconcile side effect is absorbed, and reported (since 2026-11-05).** When a reconciling
> read drives an operation or work order to COMPLETE, the handler then runs six side-effect legs over
> those transitions before it commits: `audit`, `events`, `parent_advance`, `scheduling`,
> `inventory_effects` and `cost_rollup`. Each leg absorbs its own exception, so the GET still returns
> **200**, and that leg's remaining writes are skipped. The failure used to be swallowed with no trace
> (`except Exception: pass`). It is now an **ERROR** log line with the traceback, carrying
> `reconcile_step`, `company_id`, `user_id`, `work_order_ids` and `operation_ids`. With `SENTRY_DSN`
> set it is also a Sentry event tagged `reconcile_step`, `company_id` and, where known, `user_id`.
> The `audit` leg also reports, the same way, any status-change audit row that `AuditService` failed
> to write and absorbed (it returns nothing rather than raising), naming the transitions left
> unaudited.
>
> Once a database error has left the session unusable, every later leg that touches it fails with
> `PendingRollbackError`. Those echoes are logged at **WARNING**, quoting the original error, with no
> Sentry event: the cause was already reported where it happened, and the handler's commit will fail
> and roll the whole reconcile back, so the next read retries.
>
> Transaction behaviour is unchanged. Only a failure that leaves the session unusable makes the
> handler's commit fail, which rolls the status flips back together with their audit rows. Everything
> else commits without whatever the failed leg did not write. On the `audit` leg that is a **known
> gap** (invariant 2): a status flip can commit with its status-change audit row missing, either
> because `AuditService` absorbed the write failure (it writes each row under a savepoint, so a
> `sequence_number` collision that outlasts its retries leaves the session usable) or because a
> non-database error ended the leg early. It is tracked as a follow-up: write these rows with
> `AuditService.log_required` inside a savepoint and let an audit failure abort the reconcile. Until
> that lands, the ERROR line and the Sentry event are the only record that it happened.
>
> **`PUT /scheduling/work-orders/{id}/unschedule` no longer demotes durably.** That endpoint clears
> the schedule and flips each non-COMPLETE READY operation back to PENDING. On a released work order
> that demotion is now **transient**: the next reconciling read re-promotes every operation whose
> predecessor gate passes, because promotion keys off the predecessor gate and not off whether the
> operation is scheduled. Unscheduling clears `scheduled_start` / `scheduled_end` durably; treat the
> status flip as incidental, not as a way to take work off the dispatch board. (Use ON_HOLD for that
> — it survives the read.)
>
> **An ON_HOLD predecessor blocks its own work center too.** The same-work-center allowance carries
> one carve-out: a predecessor whose status is **ON_HOLD** blocks from **any** work center, its own
> included. A hold is a quality or material stop, so while item 3 of a batch is held its siblings stop
> being startable rather than staying on the dispatch board around the problem. Because the predicate
> is shared, this **tightens clock-in as well** — `POST /shop-floor/clock-in`,
> `/shop-floor/operations/{id}/start|complete`, the two office verbs, and the scanner resolver all
> read it, and a hold that took the pool off the board while a badge scan could still start a sibling
> would be no stop at all. **Exception:** on a **laser** WO a held nest still does not block its
> siblings — the laser exemption short-circuits the whole predicate before this carve-out is reached.
>
> **Every live predecessor gate now calls the one shared predicate — no inline copies remain.**
> This landed in two steps. First the **office** verbs: `POST /work-orders/operations/{id}/start` and
> `…/complete` each held an **inline copy** passing `allow_same_work_center=False` while the shop-floor
> twins passed `True`, so the office refused an operation the floor would happily start; both were moved
> onto `operation_action_gates.operation_blocked_by_predecessors` (what clock-in and the scanner
> resolver already used). Then, with `081`, the **shop-floor** verbs: `PUT /shop-floor/operations/{id}/start`
> and `POST /shop-floor/operations/{id}/complete` still carried inline copies of their own, hard-coding
> `allow_same_work_center=True`. Left alone, those two would have kept **pooling on the operator's
> primary start and complete verbs while the board and every other gate honored a work order's
> sequenced setting** — an operation hidden from the dispatch board but startable by badge scan. Both
> now call the shared predicate too. So the per-work-order pool/routing setting, the ON_HOLD carve-out,
> and the laser dispatch-pool exemption hold identically on **every** live gate: both office verbs,
> `PUT /shop-floor/operations/{id}/start`, `POST /shop-floor/operations/{id}/complete`,
> `POST /shop-floor/clock-in`, the queue's check-in-state read, and `POST /scanner/resolve-action`.
> The refusal shape is unchanged: **400**
> `{"detail": "Previous operations must be completed first"}`.
>
> **`POST /work-orders/operations/{id}/start` is now role-gated** to **Admin / Manager / Supervisor /
> Quality**, matching its office twin `…/complete`. It previously carried **no** role gate at all
> (`get_current_user`), so any authenticated tenant user — **Viewer included** — could stamp
> `actual_start` / `started_by`, drive the work order to IN_PROGRESS, and write tamper-evident audit
> rows. The gap predates this work but was masked while the stricter office gate refused nearly every
> operation such a user could reach; with same-work-center operations promoting together, the reachable
> operations are exactly the ones the gate no longer refuses. An Operator gets **403** here and is
> unaffected in practice — the shop-floor `PUT /shop-floor/operations/{id}/start` and the kiosk stay
> open to operators by design (since P0.4, 2026-11-13, the shop-floor verb refuses Viewer and
> Shipping). See `docs/RBAC_PERMISSIONS.md` → Work Orders.
>
> **Releasing work orders.** `POST /work-orders/{id}/release` and `POST /work-orders/bulk-release` are
> both **Admin / Manager / Supervisor** (superuser and Platform Admin pass `require_role` as everywhere)
> and run one implementation, `services/work_order_release_service.py`, so the two cannot disagree
> about what a release is. A release checks exactly two things, before any write: the work order is
> **DRAFT** (`Only draft work orders can be released`) and it has **at least one operation**
> (`Work order must have at least one operation`), both **400** on the single route. **Nothing else
> gates it** — no material, blocker or readiness check. The part readiness read
> (`GET /setup/readiness/part/{part_id}`) and `GET /work-orders/{id}/material-requirements` are
> advisory; release does not consult them. A release sets RELEASED with `released_by` /
> `released_at`, runs the opt-in estimated-cost rollup (best-effort — it never blocks a release),
> promotes every startable PENDING operation to READY (each emitting `operation_ready`), emits
> `work_order_released` (best-effort; it fans out the `wo.released` notification) and writes one
> `work_order` `STATUS_CHANGE` audit row (`draft` → `released`) in the same transaction as the status
> change. After the commit it runs scheduling and the realtime broadcasts.
>
> **Releasing several work orders at once — `POST /work-orders/bulk-release`.** Body
> `{"work_order_ids": [41, 57, 41]}`: 1–50 positive ids, `extra="forbid"` (a misspelled key is **422**,
> never a silently empty request). Repeats count toward the 50 and are de-duplicated server-side, the
> first occurrence kept. Once the body validates the answer is **200** — a role outside the three
> is **403** and a malformed body **422**, as usual — with one result per distinct id, in the
> de-duplicated request order, unless the whole request fails after the per-item phase (see below):
>
> ```json
> {
>   "results": [
>     {"work_order_id": 41, "work_order_number": "WO-10001", "status": "released", "detail": null},
>     {"work_order_id": 57, "work_order_number": null, "status": "error", "detail": "Work order not found"}
>   ],
>   "released_count": 1,
>   "error_count": 1
> }
> ```
>
> Read `released_count` / `error_count` and each `status`, never the HTTP code. An item's `detail` is
> the single route's own text: `Only draft work orders can be released`,
> `Work order must have at least one operation`, or `Work order not found` — the **same** result, with
> `work_order_number: null`, for an id that is another company's, soft-deleted or absent, so the batch
> is no existence oracle. A per-item concurrent write — a stale version, or a lost lock race (deadlock
> 40P01 / serialization 40001) — gets the app-wide optimistic-lock text (`This record was modified by
> someone else. Refresh and try again.`), the text the single route answers for the same race as a
> whole-request 409, and any other per-item database failure gets `Work order could not be released.
> Refresh and try again.` (never the driver's message). Those two are bulk-only retry texts. One item's
> refusal or failure never undoes another's release. A failure **after** the per-item phase — writing
> the deferred audit rows, or the single commit — fails the **whole** request (**409** on a lost lock
> race, otherwise 5xx) and saves nothing, so no release can land without its audit row; retry the
> batch.
>
> - **One transaction, per-item savepoints.** Each id is released inside its own savepoint and the
>   route commits once. Every released work order gets exactly what the single route writes: the same
>   `STATUS_CHANGE` audit row and the same `work_order_released` event. **The `wo.released`
>   notification therefore fans out once per released work order** — releasing 50 sends 50, not one
>   summary. A refused item's events are dropped with its savepoint (the notification outbox enqueues
>   only at the outermost commit), so it notifies nobody.
> - **Lock order.** The route reads which ids are live (unlocked, tenant-scoped, soft-delete filtered),
>   then releases the live targets in ascending work-order id order. Inside each item's savepoint it
>   row-locks that job's operations (ascending id) and then the work order, both `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`
>   (the strength the release's own updates take, so an insert's foreign-key check on the job does not
>   queue behind it), before writing anything. The audit rows are written only after the last release,
>   so the global audit hash-chain lock is the last lock the request takes. Two overlapping bulk
>   releases lock in the same order. A writer that locks the work order first (the single release,
>   `PUT /work-orders/{id}`, force-complete, scheduling) can still deadlock with **one** item; Postgres
>   rolls that item back to its savepoint, it fails alone with the retry text above, and every other
>   item is unaffected.
> - **After the commit**, one tenant-scoped scheduling run covers the union of the released work
>   orders and their work centers. Broadcasts go out per released work order on the work-order and
>   dashboard channels (`work_order_released`), plus **one shop-floor push per distinct work center**
>   carrying `work_order_ids` (a list), where the single route sends one per work center carrying
>   `work_order_id`. A scheduling failure at this point is logged and reported and the route still
>   answers **200**: the releases are already committed.
> - **Not an MCP tool.** The route is in `catalog.EXCLUDED_OPERATIONS`, so `release_work_order`
>   stays an agent's only release door, one job per call (see [MCP door](#mcp-door-mcp)). The route
>   itself has no API-token refusal: a full API token whose user holds one of the three roles can call it
>   on `/api/v1` like the single route, and a read-only token is refused as for every write.
>
> In the app this is the Work Orders list: on the desktop table a user who can release gets a checkbox
> on each **draft** row (select-all covers the drafts loaded on the current page; the grouped view
> shares one selection across its group tables), and **Release N** asks for confirmation, then reports
> a success, a warning naming each refused work order with its `detail`, or an error, and reloads the
> list. The client sends at most 50 and stays non-optimistic. The mobile card list has no bulk
> selection. See `docs/RBAC_PERMISSIONS.md` → Work Orders.
>
> **Draft and on-hold work orders refuse every start (owner ruling 2026-11-05).** The floor cannot
> start work on a job a supervisor has not released, or on one a supervisor has put on hold. One pure
> helper, `operation_action_gates.work_order_start_blocker`, decides the work-order half of the start
> gate, and every start path calls it — there are no inline copies: `POST /shop-floor/clock-in` (kiosk,
> crew JOIN, desk Check In, Time Clock, and paper back-entry — `source = "backfill"` has **no**
> exemption), `PUT /shop-floor/operations/{id}/start`, `POST /work-orders/operations/{id}/start`, the
> READY auto-start branch of **both** complete verbs, the generic `PUT /work-orders/operations/{id}`
> when it writes `status: in_progress` (a hand-set start) or raises a not-started operation's
