>   completion-time `BACKFLUSH_DEMAND_REFUSED` is the **net** behind it, *not* a second gate.
>   A 409 here would also block its own remedy: correcting a blocking unit mismatch is
>   documented as `PUT /bom/items/{id}`, which refusing on an armed part would make impossible
>   without first disarming. The warning states that a re-check is needed; it does not perform
>   one (re-running the readiness explosion on every line write would put the resolution
>   layer's verdict on the write path, which is exactly the coupling that layer avoids).

> **The three multi-level reads are tenant-scoped (invariant #1).** `GET /bom/{id}/explode`,
> `GET /bom/{id}/flatten`, and `GET /bom/{id}/where-used` resolve the top-level BOM against the
> active company only — a foreign or unknown id is a flat **404** ("BOM not found"), never an
> existence confirmation. The scoping runs all the way down: every sub-BOM lookup in the recursive
> explosion carries `company_id`, so the walk cannot descend into (or leak the structure of) another
> company's BOMs even through a corrupt/mis-parented line; `where-used` joins its BOMItem scan to
> BOM and filters `company_id`, so foreign parents never appear; and the circular-reference check on
> `POST /bom/{id}/items` walks only the active company's BOMs. Previously all of these were
> unscoped reads.

> **Part names on BOM responses are resolved tenant-scoped, not through the ORM relationships.**
> `BOM.part` and `BOMItem.component_part` both join on the foreign key alone and carry no
> `company_id` predicate, so on a mis-parented row (a residual foreign key — no supported write path
> creates one) they materialise **another company's** `Part` and every response builder printed its
> part number, name and revision straight back to the caller. Both the assembly's part and every
> line's component are now resolved through one batched, company-scoped read; a part that does not
> resolve renders as `null` (`part`, `component_part`) rather than as someone else's. This covers
> `GET /bom/`, `GET /bom/{id}`, `/by-part`, `/explode`, `/flatten`, `/where-used`,
> `PUT /bom/items/{id}`, `GET /work-orders/{id}/material-requirements`,
> `GET /work-orders/preview-operations/{part_id}`, and the `bom` / `routing` result titles on
> `GET /search`. The **write** side was already scoped. Clients must treat `part` and
> `component_part` as nullable on every one of these responses.

#### BOM Item Schema

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "bom_id": 10,
  "part_id": 123,
  "quantity": 2.0,
  "position": 1,
  "is_optional": false
}
```

#### BOM line unit of measure

> ⚠️ **BEHAVIOUR CHANGE on shipped endpoints, 2026-07-27 (owner decision).** What the server
> stores for a BOM line that arrives **without** a `unit_of_measure` changed. **Before:** the
> literal `"each"`, from a schema default. **After:** the **component part's own**
> `unit_of_measure`. Same request, different stored value. No client change is required and
> no request is newly rejected — but a client that relied on omission meaning `"each"` no
> longer gets it, and **existing rows were not rewritten** (see the [report](#get-bomuom-mismatches--the-pre-arming-remediation-worklist)
> immediately below).

A BOM line's `unit_of_measure` is **optional on input**. When it is omitted, the server
resolves it to the component part's own; the literal `"each"` survives only as the last
resort — when the component cannot be resolved, or has no unit of its own. **A stated value
always wins**, so this resolves an *absence* and never second-guesses a caller. The two
document importers additionally normalise a stated value (`ea` → `each`, `lbs` → `pounds`)
exactly as they always have; the two JSON paths still store the client's string verbatim.
The **response** field stays non-null and its type is unchanged.

Applies to every BOM-line write path: `POST /bom/` (lines supplied inline),
`POST /bom/{id}/items`, `POST /bom/import/commit` and `POST /bom/import`.
`PUT /bom/items/{id}` is the one exception and deliberately so — **it is not a
backfill**: a request that does not mention `unit_of_measure` leaves the stored value
untouched, and only an explicit clear (`null` or `""`) is read as "no stated unit" and
re-inherits from the component.

Why the default was wrong rather than merely arbitrary: `unit_of_measure_mismatch` is a
**blocking** backflush diagnostic that reads a stored unit as a *stated claim*. Nothing in
the platform converts units, so a line stating `each` against a part stocked in `sheets`
would issue the wrong quantity of the right material — the diagnostic refuses
`Part.backflush_components` at opt-in (**409**) and refuses that component at completion.
Against a real sheet-metal BOM set that fired on a value nobody had chosen. **The fix was the
default; the severity was deliberately left alone.**

#### BOM line `scrap_factor` — a fraction, bounded `0 ≤ scrap_factor ≤ 1`

`scrap_factor` is a **fraction**, not a percentage: `0.05` is a 5% allowance. Entering `5`
meaning "5%" is the natural mistake, and it used to be accepted and stored as a 500%
allowance. `BOMItemBase` / `BOMItemUpdate` now bound it `ge=0, le=1`, so an out-of-range value
is a **422** naming the bound on `POST /bom/` (lines supplied inline), `POST /bom/{id}/items`
and `PUT /bom/items/{id}`. The ceiling matches `chk_bom_items_scrap_factor_range`, the DB CHECK
migration `080_restore_stamped_over_con` restored; without it the same request would fail as an
`IntegrityError` **500** at flush. The two document importers are unaffected — their schema has
no `scrap_factor` field, so an imported line always takes the `0.0` default.

Note the asymmetry with BOM-line **`quantity`**, which stays bounded at the API (`gt=0`) but
deliberately carries **no** DB CHECK: a non-positive quantity must remain *representable* so the
blocking `zero_bom_quantity` / `negative_bom_quantity` backflush diagnostics can surface it for a
human to correct. See `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` → Database Migrations for why that exclusion is
deliberate.

#### `GET /bom/uom-mismatches` — the pre-arming remediation worklist

Existing lines are **not rewritten** — this series is correct-forward and does not backfill —
so lines written before the default changed keep their stored `"each"` and still block. This
endpoint is how a human finds and corrects them.

| Query param | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `part_id` | – | Only lines on this assembly part's **own** BOM. Does **not** follow nested sub-assembly BOMs, which a readiness check *does* reach — so the **unfiltered** report is the authoritative pre-arming worklist |
| `bom_id` | – | Only lines on this BOM |
| `component_part_id` | – | Only lines naming this component part |
| `active_only` | `true` | Only active BOMs — the ones a backflush actually reads |
| `skip` / `limit` | `0` / `100` (max `500`) | Paging over the matched set |

Response: `{ total, returned, truncated, items[] }`, each item carrying `bom_id`,
`bom_revision`, `bom_status`, `bom_is_active`, `part_id`, `part_number`, `bom_item_id`,
`item_number`, `component_part_id`, `component_part_number`, `component_part_name`,
`component_is_deleted`, `line_unit_of_measure`, `component_unit_of_measure` and
`blocks_backflush`.

- The comparison is `models.part.uom_disagrees`, the **same predicate the blocking diagnostic
  uses**, so the report and the gate cannot list different rows. Comparison is exact-label:
  `ea` does **not** satisfy `each` — normalise the stored value rather than expecting the gate
  to accept it.
- A blank unit on **either** side is not a disagreement and is not reported.
- `blocks_backflush` is `false` on alternate / optional / reference lines: the backflush never
  issues those, so they raise no diagnostic and refuse nothing. Work them last.
- **`blocks_backflush: true` answers the LINE, not the whole tree — it can over-promise.** It is
  computed from the line's own type alone. A line sitting inside a `make` sub-assembly's BOM
  reports `true`, but `make` subtrees are walked exclude-only and collect no per-line
  diagnostics, so that line refuses nothing when the *parent* assembly is armed (its children
  were consumed when the sub-assembly was built). Treat `true` as "worth correcting", not as
  "this is what is refusing my part" — the authoritative list of what actually refuses a given
  part is `blockers` on `GET /parts/{part_id}/backflush-readiness`.
- Soft-deleted component parts are **included** (flagged by `component_is_deleted`), because
  the readiness explosion resolves them on purpose; filtering them out would hide a row that
  still blocks.
- `truncated: true` means the scan hit its candidate ceiling and `total` is a **floor**, not a
  count — narrow the filters and run it again.

##### Where this is worked — the **BOM Unit Mismatches** screen

The report shipped API-only in PR 4.5 and **is no longer API-only**. It has a UI at
**`/bom/uom-mismatches`**, reachable from the sidebar under **Engineering → BOM Unit
Mismatches** (directly after *Bill of Materials*). Route and nav entry are both gated on
`boms:edit` — **Admin / Manager / Supervisor**, exactly the endpoint's own
`require_role([ADMIN, MANAGER, SUPERVISOR])` — so a role that cannot act on a row neither sees
the link nor gets past the route guard by deep-linking. Client method:
`api.getBOMUomMismatches(params)` in `frontend/src/services/api.ts`, typed by
`BOMUomMismatchReport` / `BOMLineUomMismatch` / `BOMUomMismatchParams` in
`frontend/src/types/index.ts`; the page is `frontend/src/pages/BOMUomMismatches.tsx`.

What the screen is, and what it deliberately is not:

- **Read-only — it finds rows and hands off.** There is no inline BOM-line editor. Every row
  deep-links to `/bom?id={bom_id}` for the correction and to `/parts/{part_id}` for that
  assembly's own readiness. The original reason was that BOM-line create/update/delete wrote
  **no audit rows at all**, so making this screen the primary remediation flow would have put a
  compliance-critical correction on an un-audited endpoint. **That blocker is now closed** —
  all three verbs audit as `bom_line` (see [BOM line writes](#bom-line-writes)) — so an inline editor
  is no longer refused on compliance grounds; it is simply not built. Corrections stay on the
  BOM screen, where they already were.
- **Server-paged** (50 rows/page over `skip`/`limit`), so column sort is deliberately
  unavailable — sorting one page of a server-paged set reorders a window, not the worklist.
- **Filters live in URL params** (`part_id`, `bom_id`, `component_part_id`, `active_only`,
  `page`), so a filtered worklist is linkable and survives a reload. All five are parsed with
  the same strict guard — a positive integer or nothing — so a hand-edited `?page=1.1` cannot
  become a fractional `skip` the endpoint 422s, and `?page=2.5` cannot become a silently
  non-aligned window. The two part pickers search with `active_only: false` on purpose: a
  mismatch can name an inactive or soft-deleted component, and a picker that could not select
  one could not filter to the very rows this report exists to disclose.
- **`truncated` is surfaced loudly** — an amber banner above the table, and the count tile
  renders `≥ N` with the subtitle *"Floor — scan ceiling hit"*. Read as: the total is a
  **floor, not a count**, and this page is not evidence that a part is clean. Narrow the
  filters and run it again.
- **`blocks_backflush` is labelled "Line effect"**, valued *Would be issued* / *Never issued* —
  never "blocking your part", because `true` can over-promise. A permanent panel on the screen
  states that a line inside a `make` sub-assembly reads *Would be issued* and still refuses
  nothing when the parent assembly is armed, and that an assembly filter does not follow nested
  sub-assembly BOMs — so **the unfiltered list is the authoritative worklist**. The
  authoritative *per-part* answer is the **Part readiness** link on every row
  (`GET /parts/{part_id}/backflush-readiness`) — with the caveat the panel and the link tooltip
  both state: that card renders only for a part typed `manufactured` / `assembly` or one already
  armed, so a BOM hanging off a `purchased` part opens a page with **no readiness card at all**,
  and the part type is what to correct first. The link never promises a verdict silently.
- **`component_is_deleted` rows are kept and flagged**, not filtered: a red *Deleted part* chip,
  a tinted row, and a marker in the CSV export.
- **Empty means good news only when it is the whole answer.** "No rows" has four causes and the
  screen distinguishes them, because the unfiltered copy — *"No unit-of-measure mismatches —
  every BOM line states the unit its component part is stocked in. Nothing here is blocking a
  part from being armed"* — is a **conclusion about the shop**, and it is earned only on page 1
  of a complete, unfiltered scan. A **filtered** empty result says so separately and offers to
  clear the filters. A **truncated** scan that empties a page says the scan was incomplete and
  that the page is *not* an all-clear (the amber banner alone was not enough: printed directly
  above the clean copy it read as a contradiction, and the clean sentence is the one shaped like
  a conclusion). A page **past the end of the worklist** — `?page=` is durable URL state that
  outlives the rows it was written against: a shared link, a reload after remediation, an
  active-company switch — says exactly that and offers **Back to page 1**, because `DataTable`
  replaces the whole container, pager included, with the empty state. So no empty page —
  filtered, truncated, or out of range — is ever mistaken for an empty shop.

##### The remediation sequence — run this BEFORE arming any real part

1. **Run the report unfiltered.** Open `/bom/uom-mismatches` with no filters set (equivalently
   `GET /bom/uom-mismatches` with no `part_id` / `bom_id` / `component_part_id`). Leave
   `active_only=true` — those are the BOMs a backflush actually reads. Read the count; if the
   truncation banner is up, that count is a **floor**, so narrow the filters and re-run rather
   than reporting it as a total.
2. **Correct the lines on the BOM screen.** Follow each row's link to `/bom?id={bom_id}` and
   either fix the **line** (`PUT /bom/items/{id}` — state the real unit, or send
   `unit_of_measure: null` / `""` to re-inherit the component's) or fix the **component part's
   own** `unit_of_measure` where the stocking unit is the wrong record. Both are ordinary
   audited human edits; neither is a backfill. ⚠️ Correcting the **part** re-scores every BOM
   line that names it, across every assembly — so re-run the report **unfiltered** after any
   part-side correction. Rows reading *Never issued* (alternate / optional / reference) are
   cosmetic: work them last or not at all.
3. **Re-check the part** with `GET /parts/{id}/backflush-readiness` — the backflush card on the
   part page shows the same verdict and blocker list. This, not an empty report, is the
   authoritative per-part answer: the report answers *lines*, the readiness check answers the
   *part*, and it is the same function the arming gate runs.
4. **Arm it** — `PUT /parts/{id}` with `backflush_components: true`. A part whose lines still
   disagree is refused **409** with the blocker sentences as `detail`, and that refusal is the
   control working, not a bug to route around.

Clearing this list is not a lock. Every line stays editable afterwards by the same
Admin / Manager / Supervisor tier, so an empty report is evidence about the minute it was run.
The BOM edit path is no longer *blind* — a line write warns and annotates its audit row when
the edited BOM feeds an armed part (see [BOM line writes](#bom-line-writes)) — but a warning
is not a lock either. What backs the part after
the flip is the completion-time refusal (`BACKFLUSH_DEMAND_REFUSED`), not this list.

#### BOM Import (document upload)

AI-assisted BOM/part import from an uploaded document — a separate flow from the
[Bulk Imports kit](#bulk-imports--templates-excel-migration-kit). Excel uploads are parsed
directly into a reviewable table plus a suggested column mapping (no LLM call); PDF/Word
uploads go through text extraction + LLM. See
[docs/EXCEL_MIGRATION_RUNBOOK.md](EXCEL_MIGRATION_RUNBOOK.md) Step 7 for the migration flow.

| Method | Endpoint | Description | Auth Required |
|--------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| POST | `/bom/import/preview` | Upload a BOM/part document (PDF/DOC/DOCX/XLSX/XLS), get a reviewable preview (Excel: raw table + suggested mapping; PDF/Word: LLM extraction) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/bom/import/commit` | Commit a reviewed preview payload — creates parts, the BOM, and BOM items | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/bom/import` | One-shot upload → LLM extraction → create parts/BOM items (`create_missing_parts` form flag, default `true`) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |

> **Upload cap.** `POST /bom/import/preview` and `POST /bom/import` refuse a file over **20 MB**
> with **413** before any work runs (see [AI document uploads](#ai-document-uploads)); an empty file
> is **400**.

> **Excel scanning is bounded** with the same caps as the shared Bulk Imports parser: at most
> **256 columns** are read per row, more than **10,000 collected data rows** refuses the file
> (**400**), and scanning more than **100,000 raw rows** workbook-wide refuses the file (**400**).
> Two deliberate differences from the Import Center parser: **all sheets are read** (not just the
> first worksheet), and a run of more than **1,000 consecutive blank rows ends that sheet's scan
> only** — scanning continues with the next sheet, and there is **no refusal** for data sitting
> past such a gap (BOM spreadsheets legitimately scatter data blocks down a sheet; the preview
> shows exactly which rows parsed before anything is committed). The header row is padded to the
> widest data row, so unheadered trailing data columns remain mappable in the preview.
> Corrupt/unreadable Excel returns **400** `"Could not read the Excel file. Re-save it as a
> standard Excel workbook."`. On `POST /bom/import` (the LLM path), Excel **text extraction
> degrades gracefully** at the scan cap — partial text at `"medium"` confidence — rather than
> refusing the file.

> **A partly read PDF is reported (2026-11-09).** On a PDF upload to `POST /bom/import/preview` or
> `POST /bom/import`, each page the extractor skipped or cut short (see
> [Document Text Extraction Limits](#document-text-extraction-limits)) adds a sentence to the start of
> the response's `warnings`. When too little text came back to send to the AI, the **400** detail
> `"Could not extract text from document"` becomes `"Could not extract text from document."` followed
> by those sentences, so the user sees the reason (for example, that the 90-second OCR limit ran out).
> Word and Excel uploads never produce these warnings.

> **The assembly promotion is refused when live material ties stand** (2026-08-18). Both importers
> resolve an existing part by part number and set `part_type = assembly` whenever the document is a
> BOM. When that part is currently a material/supply type **and at least one OPEN work-order material
> allocation on an UNFINISHED work order still ties it**, the promotion is **skipped** and the
> refusal sentence — the same one `PUT /parts/{id}` returns as a 409, naming the part and how many
> unfinished work orders still tie it — is appended to the response's **`warnings`**. Ties held by
> finished work orders do not refuse the promotion, for the reason spelled out under
> [Work Orders](#work-orders) → "What may be tied": they carry no live demand, and since nothing ever
> closes a tie at completion, counting them would warn on every part the shop has ever consumed. The import itself still **succeeds**: a BOM attaches by
> `part_id` and is perfectly valid on a parent still typed `purchased`, so failing an entire
> multi-record import over a step of catalog hygiene would be the worse answer. A skipped promotion
> writes **no** audit row, because nothing changed. What cannot happen is a *silent* promotion — see
> [Work Orders](#work-orders) → "What may be tied" for why a tied part must not become a produced one.

> **Commits are audited.** `POST /bom/import` and `POST /bom/import/commit` write tamper-evident
> `audit_log` entries via `AuditService` tagged `extra_data.source = "bom_import"`: one CREATE per
> part created (assembly or component), one UPDATE when an existing part is promoted to
> `part_type = assembly` (none when that promotion was refused, above), and one CREATE for the BOM
> with its items summarized on the parent row
> (`item_count` + `component_part_numbers` in `extra_data` — the same parent-row pattern as the
> WO/PO imports' audit rows). Audit rows are flushed before the terminal commit so they persist
> atomically with the import. `POST /bom/import/preview` writes nothing.
>
> The BOM row's `resource_identifier` is `"{part number} BOM rev {rev}"` — the **same** handle the
> six [BOM header verbs](#bom-header-writes) write, so an auditor pulling one document's
> `resource_type="bom"` chain sees one shape from the CREATE through every later row. Both importers
> previously wrote the **bare** assembly part number here, which made the import-born CREATE the only
> row about that BOM that did not match the rest (and omitted the revision the importer had just
> written to the row). Audit rows are immutable and are never backfilled (invariant 2), so this is
> **forward-only**: rows written before the change keep the bare shape. The discontinuity is
> one-directional — the new form *contains* the old one, and audit search matches
> `resource_identifier` with a substring `ILIKE`, so a search by part number still finds rows of both
> shapes; only a search for the full new string misses the older ones.

> **Conflicts are refused with actionable 400s** rather than silently reusing soft-deleted rows or
> dying with an IntegrityError **500**. On refusal the whole import rolls back — no partial
> parts/BOM (or their audit rows) persist. The cases: an assembly or component part number matching
> a **soft-deleted part** → `"Part 'X' matches a deleted part. Restore it from Parts (or use a
> different part number) and re-import."` (the deleted row still owns the number — same contract as
> `POST /parts/`, recoverable via `POST /parts/{id}/restore`); a **deleted BOM** on the assembly
> part → `"A deleted BOM exists for part 'X' — restore it before importing."`; an **inactive BOM**
> → `"An inactive BOM exists for part 'X' — reactivate or delete it before importing."` (previously
> an IntegrityError 500); an **active BOM** → `"A BOM already exists for assembly part 'X'"` (now
> names the part).

### Work Centers

| Method | Endpoint | Description | Auth Required |
|--------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| GET | `/work-centers/` | List all work centers | Yes |
| POST | `/work-centers/` | Create work center | Yes |
| GET | `/work-centers/{id}` | Get work center by ID | Yes |
| PUT | `/work-centers/{id}` | Update work center (an `is_active: false` flip is guarded — see note below) | Admin / Manager |
| DELETE | `/work-centers/{id}` | Deactivate work center (`is_active` → `false`; `WorkCenter` has no soft-delete mixin) — guarded, see note below | Admin |

> **Deactivation is refused while live work still references the machine (409).** `DELETE
> /work-centers/{id}` and a `PUT /work-centers/{id}` that flips `is_active` `true → false` both
> count the work center's **incomplete operations** (every operation status except `COMPLETE` —
> deliberately broader than the dispatch queue: `PENDING`/`ON_HOLD` work is off the queue today but
> would be stranded on the machine just the same) on **live** work orders (non-deleted, not
> `COMPLETE`/`CLOSED`/`CANCELLED`). Any such work → **409** with a plain-string detail carrying the
> total, a per-status breakdown (ready → in progress → pending → on hold), and the remedy:
> `"Cannot deactivate LSR-1: 3 operations still have live work here (2 ready, 1 in progress). Move
> them to another machine (Dispatch Board -> Move to machine) or complete them first."` (singular
> grammar when the count is 1). The guard runs **before** anything mutates — a refusal leaves the
> row untouched — and a repeat `DELETE` of an **already-inactive** work center that still holds
> live work also 409s (previously an unconditional 200; nothing endorses the stranded state).
> Reactivation (`false → true`) is never guarded. Work stranded by a pre-guard deactivation
> surfaces on the dispatch board as a flagged read-only column — see Shop Floor →
> `GET /shop-floor/dispatch-board`.
>
> ⚠️ **`GET /work-centers/` caches per company, and the key used to be install-wide.** The
> default-parameter response is cached for 15 minutes. The query was always scoped to the
> caller's company; the cache key was the bare `work_centers:list`, so the first tenant to
> warm it had its machine roster served verbatim to **every other tenant** for the duration —
> a cross-tenant disclosure with no query defect anywhere near it. The key now carries the
> company id. Invalidation is unchanged and still a blanket wipe (`work_centers:list*`, which
> still matches the scoped keys): over-invalidation costs one recomputation, under-invalidation
> serves a stale roster. Note the cache no-ops entirely when Redis is not configured, which is
> why the regression tests drive the cache layer directly rather than relying on the endpoint.
>
> **Every state-changing work-center endpoint writes tamper-evident `audit_log` rows.** `PUT`
> logs a `work_center` `log_update` with a full before/after column diff; `DELETE` logs the
> `is_active` flip. Both self-suppress when nothing actually changed (a no-op update, or a
> `DELETE` of an already-inactive row — no fabricated diff on the hash chain). `POST
> /work-centers/` logs a `log_create` matching the CSV importer's row minus its
> `extra_data.source = "import"` marker, which is what distinguishes the two doors. `POST
> /work-centers/{id}/status` logs a `log_status_change` carrying old and new status; because
> `log_status_change` does **not** self-suppress the way `log_update` does, a request that
> restates the current status short-circuits — no write, no audit row, no broadcast.
>
> **RBAC on `POST /work-centers/{id}/status` was tightened to Admin / Manager** (it previously
> accepted any authenticated user in the tenant). It is the only writer of `current_status`
> outside the CSV importer, and flipping a machine to `offline`/`maintenance` changes what the
> dispatch board and the operator kiosk show. The tier matches `PUT`, not `DELETE`: the flip is
> reversible, and `PUT` already lets a Manager flip `is_active`. The page's inline status
> `<select>` is gated to the same role set client-side and renders as a read-only badge for
> everyone else, so a control the server will refuse is not offered. That client gate is
> **defense in depth, not the primary gate**: `/work-centers` is already route-guarded on
> `admin:settings` (`App.tsx` → `routeAccessRequirements`), which resolves to platform_admin
> + admin — a *narrower* set than these endpoints allow, so a **Manager can call the endpoint
> but cannot reach the page**. That route/nav/endpoint tier misalignment is tracked
> separately; the client gate is what keeps the control tied to its own verb's role set when
> it is resolved. ⚠️ Inside `update_work_center_status` the `status`
> query parameter **shadows the fastapi `status` module**, so `status.HTTP_*` there raises
> `AttributeError` at request time while type-checking and importing clean; use literal int
> status codes. The parameter name is part of the API contract and is not renamed.

> **`hourly_rate` is bounded `ge=0` — a negative rate is a 422, not a stored value.** `POST
> /work-centers/` and `PUT /work-centers/{id}` refuse `hourly_rate < 0` at the data boundary
> (Pydantic `Field(ge=0)` on `WorkCenterBase` / `WorkCenterUpdate`). It used to be accepted and
> persisted; the bound matches `chk_work_centers_hourly_rate_non_negative`, the DB CHECK migration
> `080_restore_stamped_over_con` restored, so without it the same request would now fail as an
> `IntegrityError` **500** at flush instead. No other work-center field changed, and the
> 2026-07-31 prod pre-flight found zero existing rows below 0.

#### Work Center Schema

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "CNC Mill 1",
  "code": "CNC-001",
  "type": "cnc",
  "description": "Haas VF-3 CNC Milling Machine",
  "hourly_rate": 120.00,
  "is_active": true
}
```

### Maintenance (PM schedules, maintenance work orders, event log)

`app/api/endpoints/maintenance.py`, mounted at `/maintenance`.

| Method | Endpoint | Description | Auth Required |
|--------|----------|-------------|---------------|
| GET | `/maintenance/schedules` | List PM schedules (`is_active` default true; `work_center_id` or `asset_id` narrows to one target) | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/schedules/{id}` | PM schedule detail | Yes |
| POST | `/maintenance/schedules` | Create PM schedule on a work center **or** an equipment asset (`next_due_date` left blank is the company's day) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| PUT | `/maintenance/schedules/{id}` | Update PM schedule (the target is not changed here). A changed `checklist` binds the schedule's **next** work order; an open one keeps the steps it was opened with (see *Checklist snapshot* under *The PM loop*). Owner decision 2026-11-20: a full API token may move `next_due_date`, also while the schedule has an open work order; a token's only refusal here is taking `checklist` steps off a schedule whose open work order has no checklist snapshot (**403**, below) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| DELETE | `/maintenance/schedules/{id}` | Deactivate PM schedule (`is_active` → `false`; no soft-delete mixin) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/maintenance/schedules/import/preview` | Dry run of a PM schedule sheet (multipart `file`; template `maintenance-schedules`). Writes nothing | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/maintenance/schedules/import/commit` | Apply a previewed PM sheet (multipart `file` + form field `expected_source_hash`). All-or-nothing. A changed checklist binds each schedule's next work order (a row warning names an open one) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| GET | `/maintenance/work-orders` | List maintenance work orders (**pure read**, see below; `asset_id` filter beside `work_center_id`). The derived `overdue` label compares `due_date` with the company's day | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/work-orders/overdue` | Overdue maintenance work orders (**pure read**; `due_date` before the company's day) | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/work-orders/{id}` | Maintenance work order detail | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/work-orders/{id}/logs` | Log entries filed against one maintenance work order (its `started` / `completed` entries and every `POST /maintenance/log` entry carrying its `maintenance_wo_id`), newest first, each with `performed_by_name` and `filed_via_api_token` (`limit` 1…500, default 100). A work order of another company is **404**. Not on the AI-external allowlist (see *Maintenance log entries* below) | Yes |
| POST | `/maintenance/work-orders` | Create maintenance work order on a work center **or** an asset (or neither, with a `schedule_id`, to inherit the schedule's target). A `schedule_id` that already has an open work order (`scheduled` / `overdue` / `in_progress` / `on_hold`) is **409** naming it. With a `schedule_id` the work order snapshots the schedule's checklist, which its completion is judged on. `scheduled_date` / `due_date` left blank are the company's day, and the `wo_number` (`MWO-YYYY-NNNN`) year is the company's calendar year | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| PUT | `/maintenance/work-orders/{id}` | Update an open maintenance work order; `status` among `scheduled`, `overdue`, `on_hold`, `cancelled` only (**409** for `in_progress` / `completed` — use the verbs — for returning a started work order to `scheduled` / `overdue`, for changing `requires_shutdown` once started, and for changing **any** field of a `completed` or `cancelled` work order, a final record; see below). Moving it to `cancelled` settles any downtime event it holds | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/maintenance/work-orders/{id}/start` | Start (→ `in_progress`). A work-center work order with `requires_shutdown` opens, adopts or shares a downtime event — never a second open one on the machine | Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Operator |
| POST | `/maintenance/work-orders/{id}/complete` | Complete (→ `completed`, advances the linked schedule from the company's day — the response adds `schedule_next_due_date`) and resolve the work order's open downtime event. `checklist_results` omitted keeps the work order's checklist, and `notes` omitted keeps its notes (a value replaces them, `null` clears them). Any checklist item left unticked (the work order's own, or a step of its PM schedule's checklist as snapshotted when it was opened) needs `incomplete_checklist_reason` (**409** without one) and a person: an API token is **403** (see *Checklist at completion* below) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Operator |
| GET | `/maintenance/calendar` | Work orders in a date window (**capped at 366 days**) | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/dashboard` | Counts, cost, per-machine MTBF/MTTR (work centers only). `overdue_count` / `due_this_week` count work orders; `schedules_overdue` / `schedules_due_this_week` count due PM schedules no scheduled / overdue / in-progress work order covers, so a PM whose work order is on hold still counts. Those four counts come from `app/services/maintenance_due_service.py`, the one rule for these tiles and the daily PM alerts (`/work-orders/overdue` and the QMS evidence card keep their own). "Today" is the company's day (see *The PM loop* below) | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/history/{work_center_id}` | Event log for one machine, newest first, each entry with `performed_by_name` and `filed_via_api_token` (`limit` 1…5000, default 100) | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/assets` | List equipment assets (`include_inactive` default false, `search` on tag / name / type), each with `active_schedule_count` and `open_work_order_count` | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/assets/{id}` | Equipment asset detail | Yes |
| GET | `/maintenance/assets/{id}/history` | Event log for one asset, newest first, each entry with `performed_by_name` and `filed_via_api_token` (`limit` 1…5000, default 100) | Yes |
| POST | `/maintenance/assets` | Register an equipment asset. **409** on a tag the company already uses (ignoring case) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| PUT | `/maintenance/assets/{id}` | Edit an asset; `version` required (**409** if stale); only the fields sent change | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| DELETE | `/maintenance/assets/{id}` | Retire an asset (`is_active` → `false`; never a physical delete) | Admin / Manager / Supervisor |
| POST | `/maintenance/log` | File a maintenance log entry: `event_type` `inspection`, `repair`, `part_replacement`, `observation` or `note` (**422** otherwise; `started` / `completed` are the Start / Complete verbs' own). With `maintenance_wo_id` the entry takes the work order's work center or asset (a different one is **409**); without one, exactly one of `work_center_id` / `asset_id`. `event_date` at most 30 days back, never in the future. A standing API token may file entries, and the entry records it (`filed_via_api_token`). The audit row is required (**503**, nothing saved). See *Maintenance log entries* below | Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Operator |

> ⚠️ **Three write paths were returning 500 in production, two of them *after* committing.**
> `MaintenanceLog` carries `TenantMixin`'s NOT NULL `company_id` (migration `026` drops the interim
> `server_default`) and `start`, `complete` and `POST /maintenance/log` all built one without it, so
> the insert raised `IntegrityError`. `start` and `complete` had already committed the work-order
> state change in a separate `db.commit()`, so an operator saw a 500, reloaded, and found the job
> running or closed anyway — a silent partial success that left the PM event history permanently
> empty. All three now stamp `company_id` and share **one** commit with the state change, so a
> request either fully succeeds or fully rolls back.

> **Every handler is now tenant-scoped, and foreign ids 404.** Ten of the sixteen handlers took no
> company argument: `start` and `complete` resolved the work order by bare id (guessing an integer
> started or closed another company's maintenance, and `complete` then advanced whatever
> `MaintenanceSchedule` that work order pointed at), and `dashboard` / `calendar` / `history` /
> `overdue` aggregated across every tenant. `work_center_id` (create schedule, create work order,
> create log), `schedule_id` (create work order) and `maintenance_wo_id` (create log) are all
> validated against the caller's company and answer a flat **404** — never 403 — with the same
> detail a genuinely missing id gets, so the status code is not an existence oracle over another
> tenant's equipment list.
>
> **Expect the dashboard numbers to drop on a multi-company install.** They were summing every
> tenant; that is the correction, not a regression. On a single-company install nothing changes and
> a smoke test can detect neither the bug nor the fix.

> **`work_center_name` reads as `null` for a legacy cross-tenant row.** The write guards stop new
> mis-tenanted rows but do nothing about rows written before them, and the serializer's relationship
> carries no predicate — a row owned by company B pointing at company A's machine passes every
> `company_id` filter (it really *is* B's row) and used to render A's machine name straight back.
> The serializers now null the related field when its `company_id` differs; `work_center_id` stays
> visible so the row can be corrected. See the pre-deploy detection SQL in
> `docs/RBAC_PERMISSIONS.md` → Maintenance.

> **No GET persists a status change any more.** Both `GET /maintenance/work-orders` and `GET
> /maintenance/work-orders/overdue` used to walk their result set flipping `scheduled` → `overdue`
> and `db.commit()` it — a status change with no actor behind it, no reason recorded and no
> `AuditService` row (invariant 2); `/overdue` did it **unscoped**, i.e. on every tenant's rows.
> Both are now pure reads. The `overdue` label still appears in the payload (derived from
> `due_date`), so responses are unchanged. Both consumers of the signal — `GET
> /maintenance/dashboard` and the AS9100D evidence card in `auto_evidence_service` — now derive it
> from `due_date` too, which is strictly more accurate: the overdue count no longer depends on
> whether a human loaded the Maintenance page today. Both compare against the **company's local
> date** (the dashboard and the two list reads used to read the server's UTC date). The two
> figures are still not identical: the evidence card also counts every **active PM schedule** whose
> `next_due_date` has passed (see QMS Standards → *the PM evidence row now judges the PM
> schedules*), while the dashboard's `overdue_count` counts maintenance work orders only (its sibling
> `schedules_overdue` counts the due schedules no work order is being worked on — see *The PM loop*).

> **RBAC was added; there was none.** Every endpoint was a bare `get_current_user`, so a **viewer
> could create, start and complete maintenance work orders**. Reads stay open to any authenticated
> user (the `/maintenance` route is gated on `work_orders:view`, which a viewer holds). Planning
> verbs match the `work_orders:create`/`work_orders:edit` role set; performing verbs (start /
> complete / log) additionally admit **Operator**, mirroring `work_orders:complete` — the
> maintenance tech doing the work signs in as one. `require_role` always admits platform admins and
> superusers.

> **Every state change writes a tamper-evident `audit_log` row** (invariant 2 — the router
> previously wrote none at all). Resource types: `maintenance_schedule` (`CREATE` / `UPDATE`, with
> the deactivation logged as the `is_active` flip), `maintenance_work_order` (`CREATE` / `UPDATE`,
> plus `STATUS_CHANGE` on start and complete — the complete row carries `total_cost`,
> `downtime_minutes`, `actual_duration_hours`, `schedule_id`, `schedule_next_due_date` and
> `resolved_downtime_event_ids` in `extra_data`, and the old and new `notes` in `old_values` /
> `new_values` when the completion changed them, plus the unticked-checklist fields when the work
> order closes with part of its checklist undone, and that row is then **required** evidence — see
> *Checklist at completion* under *The PM loop*), and `maintenance_log` (`CREATE`, **required**
> evidence since 2026-11-20 — see *Maintenance log entries*). A completion that advances a PM schedule also writes that schedule's own `maintenance_schedule` `UPDATE` row. Rows are logged **before** the
> terminal commit so they commit atomically with the change.

> **`GET /maintenance/calendar` refuses a window wider than 366 days (400)**, and refuses
> `end_date < start_date` (400). It was the one unbounded read left in the file — `start_date` and
> `end_date` are caller-supplied and there is no `limit`, so a single request could serialize every
> maintenance work order a tenant has ever had. Same posture as the list/export bounds elsewhere.

> **`wo_number` allocation stays install-wide on purpose.** `MaintenanceWorkOrder.wo_number` carries
> a *global* unique constraint, so a per-tenant sequence would hand two companies the same number
> and the second insert would fail. The scan reads only the numbers, never row content. Since
> 2026-11-20 the number is `MWO-<year>-<NNNN>` with the **company's** calendar year (it was the
> server's UTC year, so a work order opened on the evening of Dec 31 Central was numbered in the next
> year), the allocation runs under an install-wide transaction-scoped advisory lock on PostgreSQL
> (two simultaneous creates used to read the same highest number, and the second failed the unique
> constraint), and the next number follows the highest **numeric** suffix of that year. A legacy
> number whose suffix is not a number is skipped; it used to restart the sequence at `0001`.

> **Equipment assets: a maintenance record targets a work center OR an asset (migration
> `124_maintenance_assets`).** Equipment that is maintained but is not a production work center — a
> forklift, an air compressor, a manual mill — is a `maintenance_assets` row (`asset_tag` unique per
> company ignoring case, `name`, optional `asset_type` / `manufacturer` / `model` / `serial_number` /
> `location` / `notes`, `is_active`, `version`). It is not a work center and not a calibration
> `equipment` row, so it never appears in scheduling, OEE, dispatch, the kiosk or the routing pickers.
>
> - Schedules, work orders and log entries carry **exactly one** of `work_center_id` / `asset_id`
>   (a database CHECK, `ck_<table>_one_target`, holds the same rule). Both or neither is **422**
>   (*"Give work_center_id or asset_id, not both"* / *"Exactly one of work_center_id or asset_id is
>   required"*). A work order created with neither but with a `schedule_id` takes the schedule's
>   target. A foreign or missing `asset_id` is a flat **404** *"Asset not found"*, the same posture as
>   `work_center_id`; a retired asset still resolves, so its history stays readable and correctable.
> - Every schedule, work-order and log payload now names its target: `work_center_id`,
>   `work_center_name`, `asset_id`, `asset_tag`, `asset_name`, `target_type` (`work_center` or
>   `asset`), `target_code` and `target_name`, tenant-guarded on egress like `work_center_name`.
>   Schedules also return `checklist_items`, the stored `checklist` parsed tolerantly (a JSON array of
>   strings, or one item per line for older rows) with each item's text normalized (*Checklist item
>   text* under *The PM loop*); `checklist` itself is returned as stored.
> - The dashboard's counts and cost include asset work orders; its MTBF / MTTR `work_center_metrics`
>   stay work-center only, and `GET /maintenance/history/{work_center_id}` stays a work-center read
>   (assets use `/maintenance/assets/{id}/history`).
> - Asset writes are audited (`maintenance_asset` CREATE / UPDATE; a retire is the `is_active` flip,
>   logged as an UPDATE). `PUT` takes the asset's current `version` (**409** *"This asset was changed by
>   someone else…"* when stale) and rejects unknown fields; retiring keeps the asset's schedules, work
>   orders and history (deactivate its schedules separately if they should stop coming due — the
>   Maintenance → Schedules tab's **Deactivate** row action, `DELETE /maintenance/schedules/{id}`,
>   planning roles), and `PUT` with `is_active: true` brings it back.

> **Typed fields: `usage_based` is now 422, not 500.** `frequency`, `maintenance_type`, `priority` and
> (on `PUT /maintenance/work-orders/{id}`) `status` are typed against the model enums, so an unknown
> value — the old form's `usage_based` frequency included — is a **422** instead of the `ValueError`
> 500 a hand-rolled enum conversion used to raise. Frequencies are `daily`, `weekly`, `biweekly`,
> `monthly`, `quarterly`, `semi_annual`, `annual` and `custom`; `custom` requires `frequency_days`
> (1–3650) on create, and on update whenever the schedule would be left `custom` without it (**422**).
> `name` and `title` may not be blank, an explicit `null` on an always-set field of a schedule or work
> order update is **422**, and `downtime_minutes` on complete may not be negative.

> **Maintenance work order → downtime event (migration `124`).** A **work-center** maintenance work
> order with `requires_shutdown` records the stoppage through the same helpers as `POST /downtime/`
> (`app/services/downtime_service.py`), linked by `downtime_events.maintenance_work_order_id`. **A
> machine never carries two open events for one stoppage** — OEE, the downtime summary, the analytics
> and the adoption metrics all sum `duration_minutes` without merging overlaps, so a second open event
> would count the minutes twice:
>
> - **Start** opens a downtime event on the work order's work center only when the machine has no
>   open event: preventive / predictive → `planned_maintenance` + `planned` (outside OEE availability
>   loss); corrective / emergency → `mechanical` + `unplanned` (counts against OEE and in MTBF / MTTR).
>   An **open** event no maintenance work order owns (an operator logged the breakdown first) is
>   **adopted** — linked, marked `maintenance_adopted`, and audited as a `downtime_event` UPDATE. An
>   open event **another** started shutdown work order holds is **shared**: this work order opens
>   nothing (two PMs during one shutdown, a corrective job during a PM). A work order that already owns
>   an open event (restarted from hold) opens none. The start audit row carries
>   `extra_data.downtime_event_id` and `downtime_link` (`opened` / `adopted` / `shared` / `owned`),
>   plus `downtime_shared_with` (the holding work order's number) when shared.
> - **Ending a work order** (`/complete`, or `PUT` to `cancelled`) settles each open event it owns, in
>   this order: if another shutdown work order still holds the machine down (in progress, or on hold
>   after a start, and never completed), the event is **handed over** to it, still open, so the
>   stoppage resolves once — when the last work order ends — however this one ended (a cancelled
>   adopter's hand-over keeps the event's `maintenance_adopted` mark, so if that work order is cancelled
>   too the breakdown still goes back to the machine); otherwise a **cancelled** work order hands an
>   **adopted** operator's event back to the machine, unlinked and still **open** (cancelling did not
>   fix the breakdown; the next work order adopts it); otherwise the event is **resolved**. Each hand-over / hand-back is a `downtime_event` UPDATE audit
>   row. On complete, when the request leaves `downtime_minutes` at 0, the work order records the total
>   minutes of the events it resolved (a positive value from the technician is kept; a work order that
>   handed its event on records 0, so the stoppage's minutes land once, on the last one). The complete
>   audit row lists `resolved_downtime_event_ids`.
> - **`PUT` cannot bypass the verbs** (it is also an MCP tool): `status: in_progress` is **409** (use
>   `/start`), `status: completed` is **409** (use `/complete` — findings, costs, downtime minutes and the
>   PM schedule's next due date), a started work order (in progress, or on hold after a start) cannot go
>   back to `scheduled` / `overdue` (**409**), and `requires_shutdown` cannot change once it has
>   started (**409**). Re-sending the current value is accepted. `on_hold` keeps the machine down.
> - **A completed or cancelled work order is a final record; `PUT` changes nothing on it.** Any status
>   change out of either is **409** (*"… is completed, a final record; it cannot be moved to …"*;
>   open a new work order instead). Reopening one used to let a completed work order on hold take over
>   the next work order's downtime event, which then never closed, and a second `/complete` overwrite
>   the maintenance record and advance its PM schedule again. Every other field is held the same way
>   (2026-11-17): a `PUT` that would change `checklist_results`, `notes`, `title`, `description`,
>   `scheduled_date`, `due_date`, `priority`, `assigned_to` or `requires_shutdown` is **409**, a plain
>   string naming the fields — *"Maintenance work order MWO-… is completed, a final record; its
>   checklist_results, notes can no longer change. Add a later note as a maintenance log entry on the
>   work order, or open a new maintenance work order for further work."* — raised before any write.
>   Until then only the status was held, so a planning role or a token could re-tick a completed PM's
>   checklist after the fact: the very steps `/complete` demands a written reason to leave unticked
>   (*Checklist at completion* below). `notes` is refused too, because `/complete` writes them as part
>   of the completion record; a later note is `POST /maintenance/log` with the work order's
>   `maintenance_wo_id` — a dated `maintenance_logs` row signed by its author (`performed_by`), filed
>   under the work order's own machine or asset, with its own audit row — not an edit of the record.
>   On the Maintenance page that is **Add log entry** in the work order's detail view (*Maintenance
>   log entries* below). A value identical to the record's is an echo, not a
>   change, and is accepted (enums by value, `requires_shutdown` by truth — a legacy `null` reads as
>   `false` — `title` trimmed, as the request's is, and everything else exactly as stored, other text
>   not normalized); on a completed or cancelled work order such a request writes nothing (no update,
>   no audit row) and returns the work order unchanged. Open work orders are unaffected, and the
>   Maintenance page offers no edit on a completed or cancelled row. What a final record reports it
>   was judged on holds too (migration `132`): its `schedule_checklist_items` are the checklist
>   snapshot it carries, so a later schedule edit or PM import does not change them (*Checklist
>   snapshot* under *The PM loop*; a record finished without one is in *Known gaps*).
> - **An operator report cannot double it either.** `POST /downtime/` on a machine a maintenance work
>   order already holds down (its event is open, the work order in progress or on hold after a start)
>   is **409** naming the work order and the open event: the stoppage is already being recorded, and
>   it ends when that work order is completed or cancelled. An operator's report filed *before* the
>   start is adopted, as above.
> - An **asset** work order never records downtime, and neither does a legacy work order whose
>   `work_center_id` points at another company's machine. Each opened / resolved event writes its usual
>   `downtime_event` audit row and emits the same `downtime_started` / `downtime_resolved`
>   operational event an operator report does (the `downtime_started` payload adds
>   `maintenance_work_order_id`). Start and end row-lock the work order and then the work center, so
>   concurrent starts / ends on one machine are serialized and cannot both open an event.
> - **Schedule target.** `POST /maintenance/work-orders` with a `schedule_id` and an explicit
>   `work_center_id` / `asset_id` that is not the schedule's is **409** — completing the work order
>   advances that schedule's due date. Leave both empty to inherit the schedule's target.

> **Maintenance log entries: `POST /maintenance/log` and the log reads (owner decisions
> 2026-11-20).** A log entry is a dated `maintenance_logs` row signed by its author (`performed_by`):
> an inspection, repair, part replacement, observation or note against a machine or an asset,
> optionally filed against a maintenance work order. Its `maintenance_log` CREATE audit row is
> **required** evidence: if it cannot be written the request is **503** *"The audit record for this
> maintenance log entry could not be saved; nothing was saved."* and no entry is saved.
>
> - **`event_type` is a fixed vocabulary:** `inspection`, `repair`, `part_replacement`,
>   `observation`, `note`. Anything else is **422**, `started` and `completed` included: those entries
>   are written only by the work order's `/start` and `/complete` verbs, so no caller can file a
>   "completed" entry that no completion produced. The column is still free text (`String(50)`), so a
>   legacy row with any other value reads as stored.
> - **A work order's entry takes the work order's target.** With `maintenance_wo_id` (an open or a
>   finished work order: a later note on a completed one belongs here), leave `work_center_id` and
>   `asset_id` empty, or give the work order's own. A different one is **409** *"A log entry on
>   maintenance work order MWO-… is filed against that work order's own work center or asset. Leave
>   the work center and asset empty to use it, or file the entry without the work order."*, because
>   the history reads file each entry under its target and the work would land in the wrong machine's
>   history. A `maintenance_wo_id` of another company is **404** *"Work order not found"*. The
>   inherited target is still resolved inside the caller's company, so a legacy work order whose
>   target belongs to another company is a flat **404** too, never history filed against a foreign
>   machine. Without a work order, exactly one of `work_center_id` / `asset_id` is required
>   (**422**, both or neither).
> - **Date, cost, description.** `event_date` (UTC; a value carrying an offset is converted) defaults
>   to now, may be at most 30 days back (**422** *"event_date can be at most 30 days back."*) and not
>   in the future (**422** *"event_date cannot be in the future."*; five minutes of clock skew is
>   allowed). `cost` is 0 to 10,000,000. `description` is trimmed, required (blank is **422**) and
>   at most 4000 characters.
> - **Who may file one.** Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Operator, the performing tier. A read-only or
>   AI-external token is refused by its own gate (**403**), as on any write. A standing (full) API
>   token may file entries (owner decision 2026-11-20), and the entry itself records that it did
>   (migration `133`): `maintenance_logs.api_token_id` holds the token's row, every log payload
>   serves it as `filed_via_api_token: true`, and the Maintenance page's timeline tags the entry
>   *via API token*. `performed_by` is still the token's bound user, and the audit row also carries
>   `extra_data.credential`. An entry a token filed before migration `133` reads
>   `filed_via_api_token: false`; for those the audit row's `extra_data.credential` is the only
>   record of the token (never backfilled).
>   - **An MCP agent on a person's own JWT** is covered by the same decision: `create_log` stays an
>     MCP tool, and the entry is attributed to that person (`performed_by`, `filed_via_api_token:
>     false`, no credential marker), indistinguishable from one the person filed in the app. That is
>     unlike a work-order comment and Hank's `add_note`, which are people-only for an agent on any
>     credential. This half was not separately put to the owner and is to be confirmed with them.
> - **Reads.** `GET /maintenance/work-orders/{id}/logs` (any authenticated role; the MCP tool
>   `list_work_order_logs`) returns `{maintenance_wo_id, wo_number, logs[]}`: the work order's own
>   `started` / `completed` entries and every entry filed with its `maintenance_wo_id`, newest first
>   by `event_date` (an entry with none last), then id, `limit` 1…500 (default 100). A work order of
>   another company is **404**. The two history reads, `GET /maintenance/history/{work_center_id}`
>   and `GET /maintenance/assets/{id}/history`, use the same order. Every log payload (those three
>   reads and the `POST` response) carries `filed_via_api_token` and `performed_by_name`: the
>   author's full name when the author is a user of the caller's company or a platform principal (a
>   Platform Admin or superuser working in it, whom every maintenance role gate admits), `null` for
>   a user of another company (a legacy row) or when no author is recorded.
>   - **Not on the AI-external allowlist, fail-closed.** Log text can carry what an AI-external token
>     must not be handed by default: a `completed` entry's description includes the reason a PM was
>     completed with checklist steps unticked, and entries may be text a token or an agent wrote. It
>     is not a promise that no maintenance free text reaches such a token: `GET
>     /maintenance/work-orders/{id}` is allowlisted and serves a work order's `notes` and `findings`.
> - **Maintenance page.** On the Work Orders tab a row click, or the row's **Details and log** button,
>   opens the work order's detail view: the record, its log timeline, and an **Add log entry** form
>   for Admin / Manager / Supervisor / Operator that sends `maintenance_wo_id` and no target. Rows on
>   the Schedules and Assets tabs have a **History** action for the machine's or asset's log. The
>   timeline shows each entry's author, *via API token* where a token filed it, and *recorded …*
>   when the entry was saved more than five minutes apart from its `event_date` (a backdated entry).
>   The form refuses a half-filled date and time or an invalid cost before sending, rather than read
>   it as blank ("now", or no cost): a saved entry cannot be edited.

> **PM schedule import — `POST /maintenance/schedules/import/preview` then `/commit`** (Admin /
> Manager / Supervisor). Template `maintenance-schedules`, **one row per task**; `.xlsx` or `.csv`
> through the shared parser (10 MB cap), with any title block above the header row skipped (the header
> is the first of the first 10 non-blank rows holding `task` and `frequency`). It is its own preview /
> commit pair, not an Import Center batch; Import Center's **PM Schedules** card links to Maintenance →
> Schedules → **Import PM Schedules**.
>
> - **Columns:** `task` and `frequency` are required. Each row targets **one** of
>   `work_center_code` (case-insensitive; an inactive work center loads with a warning) or `asset_tag`.
>   An `asset_tag` that matches no asset is **created** on commit when the row carries `asset_name`
>   (and optionally `asset_type`) — the preview lists it under `assets_to_create`; an existing asset is
>   never renamed or retyped. Optional: `schedule_name`, `frequency_days` (custom only),
>   `next_due_date`, `estimated_duration_hours` (0–1000), `requires_shutdown`, `priority`.
> - **Frequency:** the model's values plus the sheet spellings (`yearly` → `annual`, `semi-annual`,
>   `bi-weekly`, `every 2 weeks`…). A cadence-less value (*as necessary*, *as needed*, *as required*…)
>   **skips** that row with a warning; it is never guessed. *Bi-annual* is not accepted (it means twice
>   a year to some and every two years to others) and is a row error like any unrecognized value.
> - **Grouping:** rows sharing a target, a frequency (and `frequency_days` for custom) and a schedule
>   name become **one** schedule whose checklist is the ordered, de-duplicated task list (a JSON array).
>   Each `task` is normalized as every checklist reader normalizes it (whitespace collapsed, leading
>   bullets dropped; *Checklist item text* under *The PM loop*), and duplicates are matched on that
>   text case-insensitively: a repeat is listed once, in its first spelling, with a row warning
>   (*"Duplicate of row N's task in this schedule; listed once."*).
>   The default name is *"<target code> <Frequency> PM"* (e.g. *CNC-01 Monthly PM*), so a machine with
>   monthly and yearly tasks gets two schedules. New schedules are `preventive`; their next due date is
>   the sheet's, else today (Central).
> - **Upsert:** an existing **active** schedule with the same target and name (case and spacing
>   ignored) is updated — checklist replaced, frequency set, and next due date / duration / shutdown /
>   priority set only where the sheet fills them (a blank cell never overwrites). An inactive namesake
>   gets a new schedule plus a warning.
> - **Row errors:** both or neither target; an unknown work-center code; an unknown asset tag without
>   `asset_name`; an unrecognized frequency, priority, date or number; a custom row without
>   `frequency_days`; two rows of one schedule giving different schedule-level values; one schedule
>   name given two frequencies on one target; two active schedules already holding the name. A row
>   error marks the other rows of its schedule as not loaded.
> - **Response** (both routes): `{filename, source_hash, committed, summary{…}, rows[], schedules[],
>   assets_to_create[]}` — per-row outcome (`create` / `update` / `unchanged` / `skipped` / `error`),
>   per-schedule target, tasks, values and field `changes`, and the assets to create. The preview
>   writes nothing.
> - **Commit:** `expected_source_hash` must be the preview's `source_hash` (**409** otherwise).
>   Concurrent imports for one company are serialized and every probe re-runs against current data.
>   **All-or-nothing:** any row error is **409** with `detail = {message, errors[{row, target, task,
>   error}]}` and nothing written; a tag created by someone else mid-import is a **409** asking to
>   preview again. A commit writes one **required** audit row per created asset (`maintenance_asset`
>   CREATE) and per created / updated schedule (`maintenance_schedule` CREATE / UPDATE,
>   `extra_data.source = "pm_import"`), plus one `maintenance_schedule_import` IMPORT summary row;
>   **503** with nothing saved if one cannot be written. Re-running the same sheet changes nothing and
>   writes no audit row. File-level problems are **400**.
> - **Open work orders (2026-11-20).** A changed checklist binds each schedule's **next** work order
>   (*Checklist snapshot* under *The PM loop*). For each open work order (`scheduled` / `overdue` /
>   `in_progress` / `on_hold`) on a schedule whose checklist the sheet changes, the schedule's first
>   row carries a warning, in the preview and the commit alike:
>   - a work order with a checklist snapshot: *"Schedule '…' has open maintenance work order MWO-…;
>     it keeps the checklist it was opened with, and the new checklist applies from the next work
>     order."*
>   - a work order opened before migration `132` (no snapshot), which is still judged on the
>     schedule's current checklist: *"Open maintenance work order MWO-… was opened before checklist
>     snapshots and is judged on schedule '…''s current checklist: this import changes the steps it
>     must tick or give a reason for."* When the importer is a standing **API token** and the sheet
>     takes steps away (drops, renames or clears them), this is instead a **row error** on every row
>     of that schedule — the `API_TOKEN_SCHEDULE_CHECKLIST_REMOVAL` text plus *"(Open maintenance work
>     order MWO-… on schedule '…' is judged on the schedule's current checklist.)"* — so the commit is
>     **409** with nothing written, the rule `PUT /maintenance/schedules/{id}` applies as a 403. The
>     preview shows the same row error to a token.
>
>   The open work orders are read after the schedules are row-locked, and opening a PM work order
>   takes its schedule's row lock first, so the commit cannot miss one opened mid-import.
> - Importing a schedule creates no work order. Nothing generates due PM work orders automatically
>   today; a planner opens one with **Start PM** (next note).

> **The PM loop: a due schedule, its work order, and the roll-forward.**
>
> - **"Today" is the company's calendar day.** What each of these reads as today — the dashboard's
>   counts, the `overdue` label on `GET /maintenance/work-orders` and `/work-orders/overdue`, the
>   blank-field defaults on `POST /maintenance/schedules` and `POST /maintenance/work-orders`, the
>   year in a new work order's `wo_number`, and the date a completion stamps on its PM schedule — is
>   the day on the company's wall clock
>   (`Company.timezone`, America/Chicago when unset or unrecognized), the same day the QMS PM evidence
>   row reads. It used to be the server's `date.today()`, which on the UTC deployment turns over at
>   6 PM (CST) / 7 PM (CDT): an evening completion was stamped with tomorrow's date and pushed the next
>   due date a day late.
> - **Dashboard.** `overdue_count` / `due_this_week` are unchanged: maintenance **work orders**
>   (`scheduled` or `overdue`) by `due_date`. `schedules_overdue` / `schedules_due_this_week` count
>   **active** PM schedules by `next_due_date` (before today; today through today + 7) that no
>   `scheduled` / `overdue` / `in_progress` work order carrying their `schedule_id` covers. A covered
>   schedule is counted through that work order (by its `due_date`, or on the **In progress** tile),
>   so the two pairs never count one PM twice. A PM whose open work order is **`on_hold`** has not
>   been done, so its schedule still counts here, by the schedule's own `next_due_date` (owner
>   decision 2026-11-17); the held work order itself is on no work-order count. A held work order
>   with **no** `schedule_id` (a corrective job) is still on no tile — find it on the Work Orders
>   tab's On Hold filter. `completed_this_month` and `total_cost_month` count completions since the
>   company-local first of the month (its local midnight, compared with the UTC `completed_at`). The
>   Maintenance page's Overdue / Due This Week tiles and the dashboard's **Maintenance Due** widget
>   show the sum, the page with a *"N work orders · M PMs not started or on hold"* split. A schedule
>   on a retired asset still counts until the schedule itself is deactivated. The four due / overdue
>   counts are computed by `app/services/maintenance_due_service.py` (since 2026-11-20, unchanged in
>   meaning), the one rule for these tiles and the due / overdue alerts below, so a tile and an alert
>   cannot disagree. `GET /maintenance/work-orders/overdue` and the QMS evidence card
>   (`auto_evidence_service`) keep their own overdue reads.
> - **Due and overdue alerts (owner decisions 2026-11-20).** A daily worker cron,
>   `check_maintenance_due_job`, runs at hour 12, minute 15 in the **worker container's** zone:
>   12:15 UTC (6:15 AM Central, 7:15 in summer) while `TZ` is unset, 12:15 PM Central with
>   `TZ=America/Chicago`. Whatever the hour, it judges each active company on the company's own
>   calendar day, and sends two catalog events, both direct-dispatched (`docs/NOTIFICATIONS.md`):
>   - **`maintenance.overdue`** for every item the overdue tiles count: an active PM schedule past its
>     `next_due_date` that no `scheduled` / `overdue` / `in_progress` work order covers (a PM whose
>     work order is on hold included), and every `scheduled` / `overdue` maintenance work order past
>     its `due_date` (not started). It is `recurring`: a recipient who has an unread alert for the item
>     gets no new one; once they read it, the next daily run alerts again while the item is still
>     overdue.
>   - **`maintenance.due`** once per **cycle**, for an item due today through today + 7 (the
>     due-this-week tiles). A cycle starts when the item comes within 7 days of its due date and
>     **restarts whenever the record changes** (its `updated_at`): a completion that rolls a schedule
>     forward, or any edit. Moving a due date therefore re-announces the item with the new date, and
>     an unrelated edit inside the window re-announces it too (accepted). An item that entered the
>     window on a day the job did not run is announced on the next run. A work order opened from a
>     schedule that was already announced this cycle is not announced again.
>
>   **Recipients:** the company's active users whose `department` is exactly `Maintenance`, plus its
>   active Admins, each once (the catalog entries' `departments` and `roles`; the roles changed from
>   Supervisor to Admin). **Channels: in-app only.** No preference can turn email or SMS on for these
>   two today: neither is SMS-eligible (`PUT /users/me/notification-preferences` accepts only `sms` and
>   refuses events that are not), and neither has an email channel. **Content:** the schedule's name or
>   the work order's number and title, the due date, the day count, and the machine or asset code
>   (only when the target belongs to the same company). **Links:** `/maintenance?tab=schedules` for a
>   schedule, `/maintenance?tab=work_orders` for a work order; the page follows `?tab=` also when it is
>   already open. The Schedules list is ordered by next due date; the Work Orders list by scheduled
>   date, not due date, so a due work order is among the open ones rather than at the top. The alerts
>   create no work order. **The cron fires only where the worker's `WORKER_CRON_JOBS` selects it**:
>   see `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` → PM due and overdue alerts for the owner step.
>
>   **Known limitation:** the recurring overdue alert is keyed on the record, not the cycle. A
>   recipient who never read a schedule's overdue alert from one cycle gets no overdue alert for that
>   schedule's next cycle until they read the old one.
> - **Start PM** (Schedules tab rows and the Dashboard tab's Upcoming cards; planning roles) opens the
>   work-order form pre-filled from the schedule — title = schedule name, type, priority,
>   `requires_shutdown`, description, checklist, due date = the schedule's `next_due_date`, scheduled
>   date = today (Central) — and sends `schedule_id` with **no** target, so the server inherits the
>   schedule's (an explicit different one is **409**, *Schedule target* above). A schedule that
>   already has an open work order shows that work order's number instead. The checklist is stored in
>   the work order's `checklist_results` as a JSON array of `{"item": …, "done": false}`; the Complete
>   dialog ticks each item and sends the array back.
> - **One open work order per schedule.** The server holds the same rule as the Start PM button:
>   `POST /maintenance/work-orders` with a `schedule_id` that already has a `scheduled` / `overdue` /
>   `in_progress` / `on_hold` work order is **409** *"PM schedule '…' already has an open maintenance
>   work order, MWO-… (on hold). Complete or cancel it before opening another."* — completing either of
>   two would advance the schedule and leave the other working to a due date it no longer has. A
>   `completed` or `cancelled` work order does not count. The check runs under a row lock on the
>   schedule, so two simultaneous Start PMs serialize and the second gets the 409. **The database
>   holds the same rule** (migration `132`): the partial unique index
>   `uq_maintenance_work_orders_open_schedule` on `(company_id, schedule_id)` where `schedule_id IS
>   NOT NULL AND status IN ('SCHEDULED', 'OVERDUE', 'IN_PROGRESS', 'ON_HOLD')` (the enum's stored
>   member names). It is a backstop for a writer that skips the check: should the insert trip it, the
>   create still answers the same **409** naming the open work order (or, if none can be read back,
>   **409** *"The maintenance work order could not be saved because another one was saved at the same
>   time. Nothing was changed; try again."*), never a 500. Migration `132` refuses to build the index
>   over data that already holds two open work orders on one schedule, naming them, so none survives
>   the upgrade; see `docs/DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md` for the pre-deploy check and the remedy.
> - **Complete** on a work order with a `schedule_id` sets the schedule's `last_completed_date` to the
>   company's calendar day at the moment of completion and `next_due_date` to that date plus the
>   interval (`app/services/maintenance_interval.py`, the one implementation). Day cadences add days:
>   daily 1, weekly 7, biweekly 14, custom `frequency_days` (30 for a legacy custom row without one).
>   Calendar cadences add **calendar months** (owner decision 2026-11-20): monthly 1, quarterly 3,
>   semi_annual 6, annual 12. A day past the end of a shorter month clamps to its last day (Jan 31 +
>   1 month is Feb 28, or Feb 29 in a leap year; Feb 29 + 12 months is Feb 28), and the clamp sticks:
>   a schedule completed on time every month goes Jan 31 → Feb 28 → Mar 28 (holding the original day
>   of month would need an anchor column; the owner accepted the clamp). These used to be fixed 30 /
>   90 / 182 / 365 days, so an on-time monthly PM drifted about five days earlier a year and an annual
>   one landed a day early across a Feb 29. Nothing is recomputed at deploy: an existing
>   `next_due_date` stays until the schedule's next completion. The response's `schedule_next_due_date` is the new date (`null` when no schedule
>   was advanced); the schedule's `UPDATE` audit row reads *"… advanced by completing maintenance work
>   order MWO-…"* with `extra_data.maintenance_work_order_id`. `checklist_results` omitted keeps the
>   checklist the work order carries; a value, or an explicit `null`, replaces it.
> - **Completion notes replace (owner decision 2026-11-20).** `notes` on `/complete` follows the same
>   rule: omitted keeps the notes the work order carries (a planner's, written by `PUT`), a value
>   replaces them, an explicit `null` (or blank text, stored as `null`) clears them. It used to write
>   whatever was sent, so a completion that sent no notes wiped the planner's. When the completion
>   changes them, its `STATUS_CHANGE` audit row carries the old and new text as `old_values.notes` /
>   `new_values.notes` beside the status. When it replaces or clears notes the work order already
>   had, that row is **required evidence** -- the replaced text survives nowhere else -- so if it
>   cannot be written the request is **503** and nothing is saved (as for an unticked checklist,
>   below); adding notes where there were none keeps the ordinary best-effort row. The Complete dialog pre-fills **Completion
>   Notes** with the work order's notes and sends them only when changed (trimmed; an emptied field
>   sends `null`).
> - **Checklist snapshot (owner decision 2026-11-20, migration `132`).** `POST
>   /maintenance/work-orders` with a `schedule_id` stores the schedule's checklist as it stands at that
>   moment in `schedule_checklist_snapshot` (a JSON array of strings, read under the schedule's row
>   lock; `[]` for a schedule with no steps). Completion judges those steps, and every response serves
>   them as `schedule_checklist_items`, so an edit of the schedule's checklist (`PUT
>   /maintenance/schedules/{id}`) or a PM import binds the schedule's **next** work order — never an
>   open one, and never a completed or cancelled final record. The column is server-written only:
>   neither the create nor the `PUT` body takes it, and no response returns it under its own name.
>   Two consequences of the change:
>   - A step **added** to the schedule while a work order is open is not required on that work order.
>   - A step **removed** from the schedule while a work order is open is still required on it (a tick
>     or a reason).
>
>   A work order opened before migration `132` has no snapshot (never backfilled: the list it was
>   opened with is unknowable, and an `UPDATE` outside `AuditService` would break invariant 2). While
>   it is open it is judged on, and serves, the schedule's **current** checklist, as every work order
>   was before. Completing it writes the snapshot from the schedule steps that completion judged, so
>   the finished record stops following later schedule edits from then on; the completion's audit row
>   then lists those steps in `extra_data.schedule_checklist_snapshot`. Cancelling one (`PUT` with
>   `status: cancelled`) likewise writes the snapshot from the schedule's current steps, recorded by the
>   `PUT`'s audit row. A pre-`132` work order completed or cancelled before this deploy keeps no
>   snapshot (see *Known gaps*).
> - **Checklist item text (owner decision 2026-11-20).** Every reader of a checklist normalizes each
>   item's text the same way: a schedule's `checklist` (and its `checklist_items`), a work order's
>   `checklist_results`, the checklist snapshot, `schedule_checklist_items`, and the PM import's
>   tasks. Runs of whitespace, non-breaking and other Unicode spaces included, collapse to one space;
>   the ends are trimmed; leading bullets are dropped -- a glyph (`•` `◦` `▪` `·` `‣` `⁃`), or a `-`
>   `*` `–` `—` followed by a space. Spelling is changed, never meaning: numbering (*"1. Check oil"*)
>   and case are kept, and a mark written against a word or number keeps it (*"-X axis"*, *"-40 F"*,
>   *"\*CRITICAL\*"*). Items then **match case-insensitively**
>   wherever two lists are compared — completion judging ticks, and both API-token removal guards
>   below — so *"Check Oil"* ticks *"check oil"*, and a change of spacing, bullet or case is not a
>   removal. Where two spellings meet, the first one is displayed. The rule is one Python
>   implementation (`normalize_checklist_item` / `checklist_item_key` in
>   `app/services/maintenance_checklist.py`) with a TypeScript twin in
>   `frontend/src/utils/maintenance.ts`, held together by the shared fixture
>   `frontend/src/utils/__tests__/fixtures/maintenance-checklist-normalization.json`, which pytest and
>   Jest both run (add a case there, never in one language only). It is applied on read, not by
>   rewriting stored rows: nothing is backfilled, and the raw `checklist` / `checklist_results`
>   strings are returned as stored.
> - **Checklist at completion (owner decision 2026-11-17).** `POST
>   /maintenance/work-orders/{id}/complete` takes `incomplete_checklist_reason` (string, at most 2000
>   characters). Completing with **any** checklist item unticked and no non-blank reason is **409**
>   *"N of M checklist items on maintenance work order MWO-… are not ticked (item; item). Tick them, or
>   give a reason for completing without them."* (the first ten items are named), judged before the first write, so nothing is saved (a work order
>   in a status that cannot complete gets its **400** first). A standing API token is refused **403**
>   `API_TOKEN_INCOMPLETE_CHECKLIST` *"Completing a maintenance work order with checklist items
>   unticked must be done by a person signed in to the app, not an API token."* whenever any item is
>   unticked, whatever reason it sends — checked before the reason, so the 409's invitation to give
